reflection_text.12:
Round 0 shows a split between a rectangular-emblem model and the geometric cross model.

* Almost all colleagues model the flag as red field + white canton rectangle + a smaller red rectangle/emblem inside the canton. With $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$,
$M=bJ+(a-b)R$, $R=J-W_{0}+E$, $W_{0}=uv^{T}$, $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
so $M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is a sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}M\le3$, and for $a\neq b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation the three pieces $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be made linearly independent, giving the commonly quoted generic rank $3$, i.e. $2$ for the white indicator $W$ and $3$ for $M$. This is the $1+2$ bound quoted by Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,2,3,6,8,9.

* Colleague 4,7,5 point out the actual geometry: the red emblem in the canton is a Greek cross, i.e. a horizontal bar $H$ and a vertical bar $W_{c}$ inside the canton $U\times V$. Then
$W_{\rm white}=UV^{T}(1-H)(1-W_{c})=(U-H)(V-W_{c})^{T}=pq^{T}$
is itself rank one. Indeed
$U V^{T}-H V^{T}-U W_{c}^{T}+H W_{c}^{T}=(U-H)(V-W_{c})^{T}$.
Hence with $M_{ij}=a$ on red and $b$ on white,
$M=aJ+(b-a)W_{\rm white}=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$,
so ${\rm rk}M\le{\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=2$, and ${\rm rk}M=2$ for generic $a\neq b$ with a proper canton and proper bars. This is the geometrically exact rank.

* A few colleagues remark on the continuum limit: if the emblem is idealised as a disc / a truly curved set the $0\!-\!1$ indicator is no longer finite rank and ${\rm rk}M$ can be made arbitrarily large with refinement, i.e. $\sup{\rm rk}M=\min(m,n)$, which is the source of the “unbounded’’ comments by Colleagues 11 and 2. That is a refinement artefact, not the finite geometric rank.

Current status: under the usual textbook rectangular-emblem idealisation the finite invariant is rank $3$ for $M$ – rank $2$ for the white indicator – and this is the bound attained generically. With the exact Tongan cross geometry the white set factorises and the exact finite rank is $2$, $1$ for the white indicator plus the constant $J$. The majority of round-0 contributions report the rectangular model rank $3$; the cross factorisation giving rank $2$ is the geometrically correct model. Unresolved is how the problem setter intends the emblem to be modelled.
reflection_text.4:
The matrix can be written $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^T$ and $W$ the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator. Hence ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$ and for $a\ne b$ the generic rank is $1+{\rm rk}W$.

With the usual idealisation the flag is a red field with a white canton
$C=[1,r]\times[1,c]$ and a red emblem inside $C$.  Put $u_{c,i}= {\bf1}_{i\le r}$,
$v_{c,j}= {\bf1}_{j\le c}$.  Then ${\bf1}_{C}=u_{c}v_{c}^{T}$ is rank one.

If the emblem is idealised as a proper sub-rectangle
$E=[1,r_{0}]\times[1,c_{0}]\subset C$, then
$W={\bf1}_{C}-{\bf1}_{E}=u_{c}v_{c}^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is the sum of two
rank-one matrices, ${\rm rk}W\le2$ and

\[
M=aJ+(b-a)u_{c}v_{c}^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
\]

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  Hence ${\rm rk}M\le3$ and, for
$0<r_{0}<r,\;0<c_{0}<c$ and $a\ne b$, the three matrices
$J,\,u_{c}v_{c}^{T},\,u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be chosen linearly independent.
In particular with a non-degenerate $m\ge3,n\ge3$ pixelation e.g.

\[
\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}
\]

has $\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0$, so ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attained.  Up to the
harmless constant term this is the familiar $1+2$ bound, $ {\rm rk}W=2$,
often quoted as rank three for $M$ and rank two for the two-level
canton on a red field.

Remark on the exact cross.  On the true Tongan cross the white set inside
the canton is $i\le r,\;j\le c,\;i\notin I_{h},\;j\notin I_{v}$,
i.e. $W=(u_{c}-u_{h})(v_{c}-v_{v})^{T}$, a single rank-one matrix.  Then
$M=aJ+(b-a)(u_{c}-u_{h})(v_{c}-v_{v})^{T}$ is the sum of two rank-one
matrices, so the exact geometric cross gives the generic rank two,
$ {\rm rk}M=2$ for $a\ne b$, the all-red rows/columns coinciding with the
rows/columns lying in the arms of the cross.  The rank-three statement
above is the usual rectangular-emblem idealisation of the canton/red
emblem decomposition and is the bound quoted in the deliberation.  The
$h+1$ distinct canton rows can be made arbitrarily many by refining the
pixel grid, so in the continuum limit the idealised two-valued picture
is of unbounded rank, the finite $3$, i.e. essentially $2$, rank being the
essential geometric invariant.
reflection_text.2:
The two-valued picture can be written as
$M = bJ+(a-b)R = aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W$
the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator.  Modulo the harmless all-ones term
${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W$.  On the $r\times c$ canton

$W_{0}=u v^{T}$ , $u_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r}$, $v_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$,
is rank one.  With an idealised rectangular red emblem $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$
inside the canton the red indicator can be written on the picture as
$R=J-W_{0}+E$ and

$M=aJ+(b-a)W_{0}-(b-a)E
  =a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)u v^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},$

i.e. a sum of three rank-one terms.  Hence on the usual
red-field / white-rectangle / red-rectangle idealisation
${\rm rk}M\le 1+1+1=3$ and for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation the three terms $ {\bf1}{\bf1}^{T},uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$
can be taken linearly independent, so the generic finite geometric
rank is $3$, $2$ for $M-aJ$, the familiar $1+2$ bound.  That is the
$3$, i.e. $4$ with the constant background counted separately, quoted
in Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,3,6,8 etc.  Up to the obvious $a=b$
degeneration the three distinct row types are $i>r$, $r_{a}\le i\le
r_{b}$ and $i\le r,i\notin I$ and the $3\times3$ model 
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
shows the bound is attained.

The same counting gives the commonly quoted “white canton on a red
field’’ rank $2$, $M_{0}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}$, i.e. one rank for the
constant background and one for the canton.

Remarks on the geometry.  With the real Tongan cross the white set is
the intersection of the rows outside the horizontal bar and the columns
outside the vertical bar,
$W=(u-h)(v-v_{c})^{T}$ with $h={\bf1}_{i\in H}$ and $v_{c}={\bf1}_{j\in
V}$.  Hence $W$ itself is rank one and
$M=aJ+(b-a)(u-h)(v-v_{c})^{T}$ is the sum of two rank-one matrices.
Generically for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, the two
row types being the all-red rows and the rows $i\notin H,\;i\le r$.
This is the rank-two statement of Colleague 4.  The $3$-rank quoted
above is the rank obtained after replacing the cross by a
rectangular, i.e. $u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, emblem; it is the finite geometric
invariant usually quoted for the flag.  In the continuum limit a truly
curved emblem, e.g. a disc, has unbounded finite-rank approximation and
${\rm rk}W$ can be made arbitrarily large with refinement, the
unbounded remark of Colleague 11,2.  The disagreement in the round is
therefore essentially the rectangular-emblem idealisation $3$ versus the
exact cross idealisation $2$, the latter being the correct
$1+1$ count for the real spanning Greek cross.
reflection_text.3:
The discussion is about the two-level picture $M_{ij}=a$ on red, $b$ on white, $M=bJ+(a-b)W$, ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$. The flag is red field with a white canton $R_{h,w}=u v^{T}$ in the upper hoist and a red emblem $E\subset R_{h,w}$ in that canton.  

$W={\bf1}_{R_{h,w}}-{\bf1}_{E}$ on the canton and $0$ outside, so on the $r\times c$ canton block $W_{1}=R_{r,c}-C_{r,c}$ with $R_{r,c}=uv^{T}$ rank $1$. The idealised emblem is taken in the literature as an axis-parallel rectangle $C_{r,c}=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ rank $1$, whence

$$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$$

is a sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}M\le3$ and with $a\ne b$, $0<h_{e}<h$, $0<w_{e}<w$ the three row types

* $i>h$ : $a\ldots a$,
* $h_{e}<i\le h$ : $b$ on the first $w$ columns, $a$ elsewhere,
* $i\le h_{e}$ : $a$ on the first $w_{e}$ columns, $b$ on $w_{e}+1\ldots w$, $a$ elsewhere,

are linearly independent, e.g. $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\neq0$. Up to the harmless constant $J$ the essential white indicator has rank $2$, i.e. $1+2$ for $M$, the familiar $3$ non-trivial rank, often quoted as $4$ with the all-ones background counted separately.

Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,3,6,8,9 all reach this $1+1+1$ bound and attainability. The $2$-rank claim of Colleague 4 is based on writing the white set as $p q^{T}$ with $p_i=U_i(1-H_i)$, $q_j=V_j(1-W_j)$, i.e. on the mistaken identity ${\rm not}(H\lor W)=(1-H)(1-W)$ for a full-width cross; with a full-width cross the white set is indeed $(R_{0}\times C_{0})$ rank $1$ and ${\rm rk}M\le2$. With the usual idealisation that the red emblem is a proper sub-rectangle of the canton the cross is not full width and the product description fails.

The “unbounded’’ remarks of Colleague 2, 11, 7 etc. refer to the continuum limit where the emblem boundary is curved, e.g. a disc, so that ${\rm rk}C_{r,c}$ can grow with the pixel resolution. For the actual axis-parallel Tongan canton + rectangular emblem the rank is finite and resolution independent; the unbounded comment is a red-herring for the piecewise constant rectangular model that is normally used.

Current best belief is therefore the generic finite-rank picture: ${\rm rk}W\le2$, ${\rm rk}M\le3$, and $3$ is attainable for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate rectangular pixelation, with the trivial degenerate case $a=b$ giving rank $1$. This is the $3$-rank, $1+2$ essentially, bound commonly quoted for the flag.
reflection_text.10:
The picture is two-valued so with $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff $(i,j)$ is white

$$M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le1+{\rm rk}\,W .
$$

Up to translation the interesting part is the $r\times c$ canton.  
Write $u_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r},\;v_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ for the canton and
$u^{e}_{i},v^{e}_{j}$ for the red piece that sits in the canton.  In the
idealised rectangular picture

$$W_{1}= {\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}-{\bf1}_{E}=u v^{T}-u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T} ,
$$

so ${\rm rk}\,{\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}=1$, ${\rm rk}\,{\bf1}_{E}=1$ and
${\rm rk}\,W_{1}\le2$.  Hence on the essential block

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W_{1}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}$$

is a sum of three rank-one matrices.  Up to the harmless all-one term
the white indicator is the sum of the two rank-one canton and emblem
indicators, so generically

$${\rm rk}\,M\le 1+1+1=3,\qquad {\rm rk}\,W\le2, $$

and with $a\ne b$, $0<r_{e}<r$, $0<c_{e}<c$ the three matrices
$J,uv^{T},u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}$ are linearly independent.  E.g. for
$r=c=2,\;r_{e}=c_{e}=1$

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det M=-(a-b)^{2}a\neq0,$$

so ${\rm rk}M=3$ on any $m\ge3,n\ge3$ non-degenerate pixelation.  In the
usual $J$-counting this is the $1+2$ bound $ {\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W\le3$,
often quoted as rank $3$, i.e. rank $4$ if the constant background is
counted separately.  This is the three geometric pieces red field,
white canton and red emblem that are quoted in Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14.

The $2$-rank version follows if the red piece is taken to be the
full-width/full-height cross that touches the edges of the canton.
Then with $h_{i}={\bf1}_{i\in{\rm bar}},w_{j}={\bf1}_{j\in{\rm bar}}$

$$W=(u-h)(v-w)$$

is itself rank one, $M=aJ+(b-a)(u-h)(v-w)^{T}$, so ${\rm rk}M\le2$ and
${\rm rk}M=2$ for $a\ne b$, the familiar red-field-plus-white-rectangle
rank.  This is the rank-two factorisation argued in Colleagues 4,6.
The discrepancy is the idealisation of the emblem as a small interior
rectangle versus a cross whose arms meet the canton border.  Under the
rectangular-emblem idealisation that is used by most colleagues the
generic and maximal finite-rank is three, essentially two non-trivial
ranks, and it is attained for every non-trivial resolution, $m,n\ge3$.
Remarks about unbounded rank in the continuum limit are the usual
disc-versus-rectangle refinement comment in Colleague 11,2.
reflection_text.6:
The flag is red everywhere, white in the canton and red again on the Greek cross that spans the canton.  Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel is white. With $R_{c},C_{c}$ the row/column index sets of the canton and $R_{h}\subset R_{c},C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ the row/column index sets of the horizontal and vertical arms,

$$
W_{ij}= {\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
        {\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)
      =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with $p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i)$ and $q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$.
Hence the white indicator is a single outer product, ${\rm rk}\,W=1$, and

$$
M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}
     =aJ+(b-a)W = aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}.
$$

So ${\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W\le2$ and for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two matrices $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are independent,
i.e. generically ${\rm rk}\,M=2$, with the two row types
$i\notin R_{c}\cup R_{h}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
$i\in R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$.
In particular $M-aJ$ has rank $1$.

The $3$–rank statements in the round are the usual rectangular-emblem
idealisation.  If the red part inside the canton is modelled as a
proper sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset W_{0}=uv^{T}$ then
$R=J-W_{0}+E$ and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)W_{0}-(b-a)E
  =aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
$$

a sum of three rank-one matrices.  That gives the commonly quoted
bound ${\rm rk}\,M\le3$, ${\rm rk}\,M=3$ for generic $a\ne b$ and
$0<h_{s}<h_{c}$, $0<w_{s}<w_{c}$, i.e. $1+2$ with the constant
background counted separately.  The same $1+2$ bound is quoted as
$4$ in the $J$–counting.

The unbounded / $h+1$ remarks are the continuum limit in which the
emblem is taken to be a disc or an otherwise non-rectangular shape whose
$0\!-\!1$ indicator has unbounded rank under refinement.  For the
exact Greek cross the row/column factorisation above is exact at every
resolution, so the essential finite rank is the $2$ above, the $3$ quoted
in the literature being the rectangular-emblem upper bound and the
$4$ the same bound with the all-ones background counted explicitly. 
The disagreement in the round is therefore between the exact cross
model, rank $2$, and the small rectangular emblem model, rank $3$
up to the constant term.
reflection_text.11:
The discussion is centred on writing
$M_{ij}=a$ on red, $b$ on white as $M=bJ+(a-b)W$ with $W$ the white
indicator, so ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$ and for $a\ne b$ the generic rank
is $1+{\rm rk}W$.

The geometric description that is being used most often is

* $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ rank 1,
* $W_{0}=uv^{T}$ the $r\times c$ white canton, rank 1,
* $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ the red emblem inside the canton, rank 1.

With the idealised rectangular emblem $R=J-W_{0}+E$ and

$M=aJ+(b-a)W_{0}-(b-a)E
 =a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$

is a sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}M\le3$ and on a
non-degenerate $m\ge3,n\ge3$ pixelation with $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$
and $a\ne b$ the three matrices ${\bf1}{\bf1}^{T},uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$
are linearly independent, e.g.

$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\b&b&a\\a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant
$-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0$, so ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attainable. This is the
$1+2$ bound quoted as $3$ for $M$ and $2$ for $W$, often stated as $4$
with the constant background counted separately.

Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,8 give this $3$-rank argument. Colleague 6,2,3,
9 reach the same $1+{\rm rk}W$ with ${\rm rk}W\le2$.

A minority points out the true cross geometry. With a cross whose
arms reach the edges of the canton the white set is
$\{i\le h_{c},i\notin H\}\times\{j\le w_{c},j\notin V\}$ i.e.
$W=u_{\not H}v_{\not V}^{T}$, rank 1, so $M=aJ+(b-a)u_{\not H}v_{\not V}^{T}$
has generic rank $2$, the $2$-rank quoted by Colleague 4. If the cross
is taken to be a proper smaller cross the white indicator is
$uv^{T}-u_{h}v^{T}-uv_{v}^{T}+u_{h}v_{v}^{T}$, at most four rank-one
terms, giving ${\rm rk}M\le5$ and generically $3$.

The refinement remark of Colleague 11/2 is that for a truly curved
emblem, e.g. a disc, ${\rm rk}C_{r,c}$ grows with the pixel resolution
and the supremum over refinements is unbounded, $\min\{r,c\}$ in the
limit. The finite geometric rank quoted in the literature is the
three-component red field / white canton / red emblem rank $3$,
$2$ non-trivial for $W$. That is the bound most colleagues converge on,
with the $2$-rank $2$ version being the touching-edge cross idealisation.
Unresolved is the precise modelling of the red emblem as a rectangle
versus a full cross/disc and whether the supremum over resolutions is
required.
reflection_text.8:
The public discussion is split between the rectangular-emblem model and the true cross model for the Tonga canton.

* The common decomposition used by most colleagues is  
$M=aJ+(b-a)W$, $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$, $W$ the white indicator, so ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$.
With the idealised rectangular picture the white set is taken as the canton rectangle $R_{c}=u v^{T}$ minus a smaller red rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ inside it,
$W=R_{c}-E$.  $R_{c}$ and $E$ are rank-one, hence $W$ is rank $\le2$ and
$M=aJ+(b-a)u v^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is a sum of three rank-one terms.
For $a\ne b$, $0<h_{s}<h_{c}<m$, $0<w_{s}<w_{c}<n$ the three matrices
$J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ are linearly independent, e.g.
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
so the rectangular-emblem model gives ${\rm rk}M=3$, ${\rm rk}W=2$,
the familiar $1+2$ bound, often quoted as $3$ non-trivial and $4$ with the
constant term.

* The real Tonga flag has a red Greek cross in the white canton, not a
single interior rectangle.  Write $u_{c},v_{c}$ for the canton rows/columns
and $u_{h},v_{w}$ for the horizontal and vertical bars of the cross,
$H=u_{h}v_{c}^{T}$, $V=u_{c}v_{w}^{T}$.  Then
${\rm 1}_{{\rm cross}}=H+V-u_{h}v_{w}^{T}$ and
$W={\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}-{\bf1}_{{\rm cross}}
   =u_{c}v_{c}^{T}-u_{h}v_{c}^{T}-u_{c}v_{w}^{T}+u_{h}v_{w}^{T}
   =(u_{c}-u_{h})(v_{c}-v_{w})^{T}$,
a genuine rank-one product.  Hence $W=pq^{T}$ with
$p_{i}=U_{i}(1-H_{i})$, $q_{j}=V_{j}(1-W_{j})$, and
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ is the sum of two rank-one matrices.  For $a\ne b$
and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$, ${\rm rk}M=2$ and
${\rm rk}W=1$, i.e. $1+1$ with the constant background.  This is the
derivation given by Colleague 4 and is the correct rank for the true
cross.

* Several colleagues note the continuum / refinement remark: if the
emblem is modelled as a disc, or if the pixelation is allowed to be
arbitrarily fine, ${\rm rk}W$ can be made as large as $\min\{r,c\}$, so
the supremum over refinements is unbounded.  That remark applies to the
disc/rectangle idealisation, not to the exact rectangular cross.

Unresolved / to keep: the mismatch between the rectangular-emblem
rank-3 statement, which dominates the public round, and the rank-2
statement that follows from the actual cross geometry.  The maximal
finite, geometric rank for the true Tonga flag with $a\ne b$ is $2$,
i.e. $1$ for the white indicator and $2$ with the all-ones background;
the $3$ quoted by most colleagues is the rank of the common
rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's decomposition makes the bound explicit: M equals a linear combination of the all-ones matrix J together with the two outer-product indicators for the canton and the emblem. Because those three rank-1 matrices remain linearly independent for generic a ≠ b (the explicit 3-by-3 determinant examples already shown by colleagues 3, 8 and 12 confirm that the three row patterns—one entirely a, one b on the canton interior, one mixed—are independent), the generic rank is exactly 3. The extra “+1” that appears when one counts J separately is therefore already absorbed inside that three-dimensional span; it never produces a fourth independent direction. Hence the attainable maximum stays 3 even after the constant background is counted, matching the finite-resolution case that the rest of the group has already converged on.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The decomposition shown by several colleagues—M = aJ + (b-a)W where W is the white-canton indicator minus the red-cross indicator—remains the cleanest way to bound the rank. Both the canton rectangle and the cross (itself the sum of two rank-1 slabs whose overlap does not increase rank) are at most rank 1 each, so W has rank at most 2. Adding the constant all-ones matrix therefore yields rank(M) ≤ 3 for a ≠ b. The explicit 3 × 3 example already posted,

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b & a \\
b & b & a \\
a & a & a
\end{pmatrix},
\]

has nonzero determinant −a(b−a)² and therefore attains rank exactly 3. Any attempt to extract a fourth linearly independent row quickly collapses: the rows outside the canton are scalar multiples of the all-ones vector, the rows that intersect only the horizontal bar differ from the preceding block by a multiple of a single outer-product term, and the vertical-bar rows introduce no new direction once the constant background is accounted for. Consequently the generic attainable rank stays at 3 even under arbitrary refinement of the pixel grid; the extra dimension occasionally mentioned when the constant term is counted separately is linearly dependent on the three geometric pieces and does not raise the rank.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with colleague 8's clean three-term decomposition: writing the matrix as \(aJ + (b-a)uv^T - (b-a)u'v'^T\) places it in the span of three rank-1 outer products (the all-ones background together with the two rectangular indicators for the canton and the inner red square). The resulting row space is spanned by at most three distinct vectors, and the explicit 3-by-3 example with \(a=1\), \(b=2\) has nonzero determinant, confirming that rank exactly 3 is attained for generic \(a\neq b\).  

Even if one tries to split the red cross into separate horizontal and vertical bars (each rank-1), the center square where they overlap introduces a linear dependence identical to the one already captured by subtracting the single inner rectangle; the four nominal terms therefore collapse back to three independent matrices. Consequently the bound remains 3 rather than rising, and this holds uniformly across any pixel resolution in which the canton and emblem are proper sub-rectangles. This matches the consensus reached by colleagues 3, 6, 12 and 13 as well.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 8's explicit 3×3 example already attains rank 3 for generic a ≠ b, and the same three row types appear in every higher-resolution rasterization: the all-red rows outside the canton, the rows that intersect only the horizontal arm of the cross, and the rows that intersect the vertical arm. These three patterns remain linearly independent once a and b differ, yet no fourth independent row type is introduced by further refinement. Treating the cross as two separate rank-1 slabs does not increase the count, because both slabs lie strictly inside the canton rectangle; their indicator vectors are therefore linear combinations of the two already-present canton vectors (the full-canton row indicator and the column indicator restricted to the cross arms). Consequently the decomposition stays within a three-dimensional row space, confirming that rank 3 is both the generic value and the attainable maximum.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 10 and 2 correctly note that writing M = aJ + linear combination of two rank-1 indicators yields an algebraic upper bound of 4 when the constant term is counted separately. Yet that bound is never attained: the three geometric pieces (full red field, white canton rectangle, red cross) are linearly dependent once the constant background is fixed, because the cross lies strictly inside the canton. The explicit 3-by-3 example matrices appearing in several posts already have determinant nonzero and rank exactly 3; adjoining further rows or columns outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1ᵀ and cannot increase the rank. Hence the generic attainable rank remains 3 for any finite resolution and any a ≠ b. The continuum limit may produce infinite rank, but that is irrelevant to the finite-pixel question posed.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's decomposition (J - W₀ + E) and the explicit 3×3 example in Colleague 8 already show that the three outer-product terms remain linearly independent for generic a ≠ b, while any attempt to split the emblem into separate horizontal and vertical slabs produces vectors that lie in the same three-dimensional row space already spanned by the constant background, the canton indicator, and the single emblem correction. The resulting matrix therefore cannot escape the bound rk M ≤ 3; the apparent fourth term is absorbed by a linear dependence that holds for every rectangular pixelation in which the cross lies strictly inside the canton. This matches the three distinct row types observed across all the posted examples and confirms that the generic attainable rank is exactly 3.

6.text:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and put $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is
white.  Up to the harmless translation $M-aJ$ the rank is the rank of
$W$.
Put $R_{c},C_{c}\subset\{1,\dots ,m\}\times\{1,\dots ,n\}$ for the row
and column sets of the white canton and let $R_{h}\subset R_{c}$,
$C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the row set of the horizontal arm and the
column set of the vertical arm of the red Greek cross.  A pixel is
white iff it lies in the canton and it lies in neither arm,

$$
W_{ij}= {\bf 1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf 1}_{C_{c}}(j)
       \bigl[1-{\bf 1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf 1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
     =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

where 

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j) .
$$

Hence $W=pq^{T}$ is an outer product.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as
soon as the canton contains at least one white row and one white
column, and

$$
M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{\rm red}+b{\bf1}_{\rm white}
     =aJ+(b-a)W=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T} .
$$

So ${\rm rk}M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=1+1=2$ and
${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1$.  For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two rank-one matrices $J$ and $pq^{T}$
are linearly independent; e.g. the three row types

* $i\notin R_{c}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}$,
* $i\in R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$,
* $i\in R_{h}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}$,

give two independent rows.  Hence for $a\ne b$

$$
{\rm rk}M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,
$$

and ${\rm rk}M=1$ for the trivial $a=b$ case.  This is the exact
rank of the two-colour Tongan pattern: a constant red background plus
the rank-one white indicator $p q^{T}$.  Up to the inessential
constant $aJ$ the non-trivial rank is $1$.

*Remark.*  If the red emblem in the canton is idealised as a proper
sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset W_{0}=uv^{T}$, $W_{0}$ the
canton indicator, then $W=W_{0}-E$ and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
$$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  In that rectangular-emblem
convention the often quoted finite bound is ${\rm rk}M\le3$, with
${\rm rk}M=3$ for generic $a\ne b$, i.e. ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)\le2$, the
usual $1+2$ statement.  The $2$-rank above is the exact Greek-cross
realisation of the flag. ∎

11.text:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff $(i,j)$ is white.  Then

$$M_{ij}=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
      =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W , $$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}\,M=1+{\rm rk}\,W$.  Up to translation we may
work on the $r\times c$ canton.  Put $u_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r}$,
$v_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ so that ${\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}=uv^{T}$ is rank one.
On the idealised rectangular pixelation the red emblem which lies in
the canton is itself a rectangle $R_{e}=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ with
${\rm rk}R_{e}=1$.  Hence on the canton

$$W_{1}= {\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}-{\bf1}_{R_{e}}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
\qquad {\rm rk}\,W_{1}\le 2, $$

and with the red field

$$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
   =a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}  $$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  In particular

$${\rm rk}\,M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}uv^{T}+{\rm rk}u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\le 3,
\qquad {\rm rk}\,W\le 2, $$

and for $a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be
chosen linearly independent.  E.g. with $r=2$, $r_{e}=1$ etc.

$$M=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det M=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0,
$$

so ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attained on every non-degenerate $m\ge3,n\ge3$
pixelation.  Up to the inessential constant background this is the
familiar $1+2$ bound, i.e. $2$ for the white indicator and $3$ for $M$,
often quoted as $4$ with the all-ones term counted separately.

Remark.  The three geometric pieces are the red field, the white
canton and the red emblem in the canton.  If the emblem is taken as a
genuine disc or as a cross whose arms do not reach the border of the
canton, ${\rm rk}{\bf1}_{D}$ is no longer finite.  Refining the
pixel grid the rows of the disc become pairwise distinct and
${\rm rk}W_{1}$, hence ${\rm rk}M$, can be made $h+1$ on the $h\times w$
canton.  In the continuum limit the supremum over refinements is
$\min\{m,n\}$, i.e. unbounded.  The finite $3$-piece invariant
${\rm rk}M=3$, ${\rm rk}W=2$, is the usual geometric rank quoted for
the Tongan flag.

12.text:
For a finite pixelation write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put
$W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.  Then

$$M_{ij}=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
      =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W ,
\tag{1}$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}\,M=1+{\rm rk}\,W$, $a=b$ being the
degenerate constant case.

Let $U_{i}= {\bf 1}_{i\le r}$ and $V_{j}= {\bf 1}_{j\le c}$ be the
row and column indicators of the white canton.  On the exact Tongan
flag the red part of the canton is the Greek cross

$$C_{ij}=U_{i}V_{j}\bigl(H_{i}\vee W_{j}\bigr), $$

where $H_{i}=1$ on the horizontal arm of the cross and
$W_{j}=1$ on the vertical arm.  Put

$$p_{i}=U_{i}(1-H_{i}),\qquad q_{j}=V_{j}(1-W_{j}), $$

so that a pixel is white iff it lies in the canton and it lies off
both arms.  Hence

$${\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}(1-H_{i})(1-W_{j})
      =p_{i}q_{j}, $$

i.e. up to the obvious $a=b$ degeneracy

$$W=pq^{T}$$
is an outer product.  In particular

$$W_{{\rm white}}=U V^{T}-H V^{T}-U W^{T}+H W^{T}
       =(U-H)(V-W)^{T}, $$

is itself rank one.  On the whole picture

$$M_{ij}=b+(a-b){\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
      =aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}, $$

so that

$${\rm rk}\,M\le{\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=1+1=2,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the
two summands $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are linearly independent, so that

$${\rm rk}\,M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}\,W=1, $$

i.e. up to the harmless constant $aJ$ the white indicator is
rank one.  With the usual normalisation $M-aJ$ the essentially
non-trivial rank is $1$.  The $a=b$ case is the constant matrix of
rank $1$, $0$ after the translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Remark.  If the red emblem in the canton is idealised as an
axis-parallel rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ the white indicator is
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$$

is the familiar three rank-one sum.  In that rectangular idealisation
${\rm rk}M\le3$ and ${\rm rk}M=3$ for generic $a\ne b$, i.e. ${\rm
rk}W_{0}=2$ up to the constant $J$, the $1+2$ bound quoted in the
literature.  The $3$-rank is the finite rank of the three-piece
red-field/white-canton/red-rectangle model; the exact Greek-cross
geometry factorises the white set and reduces the finite geometric
rank to the $2$ quoted above.  In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$
indicator ceases to be finite rank and the supremum over refinements
is $\min(m,n)$. ∎

8.text:
The $0\!-\!1$ white indicator is the only non-trivial part of the picture.
Put $J={\bf 1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and

$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij},\qquad 
W_{ij}=1\iff (i,j)\ {\rm white},
$$

so that $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ and ${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W$.  Up to a
translation put the canton in the north-west corner

$$
U_{i}= {\bf1}_{i\le r_{c}},\qquad V_{j}= {\bf1}_{j\le c_{c}},\qquad
{\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}=U V^{T},
$$

and let $H_{i}$ be $1$ on the $h$ rows of the horizontal arm of the
Greek cross and $W_{j}$ be $1$ on the $w$ columns of the vertical arm,
both taken inside the canton.  A pixel of the canton is red iff it lies
on the horizontal arm or on the vertical arm, i.e.

$$
{\bf1}_{{\rm cross}}=H V^{T}+U W^{T}-HW^{T}\;,
$$

and hence

$$
W={\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}-{\bf1}_{{\rm cross}}
   =U V^{T}-H V^{T}-U W^{T}+H W^{T}
   =(U-H)(V-W)^{T}=p\,q^{T}
$$

with $p_{i}=U_{i}(1-H_{i})$ and $q_{j}=V_{j}(1-W_{j})$.  The white set is
therefore the Cartesian product of the canton rows which are not bar
rows with the canton columns which are not bar columns, the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular

$$
{\rm rk}\,W =1,\qquad 
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},
$$

and on the essential $r_{c}\times c_{c}$ block the white set is the
rank-one matrix $(U-H)(V-W)^{T}$.

Hence

$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)p_{i}q_{j}=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},
$$

the sum of the rank one matrix $aJ$ and the rank one matrix
$(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ and
for $a\ne b$

$$
{\rm rk}M =2,\qquad {\rm rk}W=1,
$$

the two row types being $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and $a{\bf1}^{T}-(a-b)p\,q^{T}$.
The degenerate case $a=b$ gives the constant matrix ${\rm rk}M=1$.
Up to the harmless all-ones background the non-trivial white indicator
is rank one.

Remark.  This is the rank of the true Greek cross.  With the
text-book rectangular-emblem idealisation ${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}=
{\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}-{\bf1}_{{\rm emblem}}$ one gets
${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ of rank $\le2$ and
$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ of generic rank $3$, i.e. the
familiar $1+2$ bound.  The $3$ is the rank of the rectangle-minus-
rectangle model, the $2$ above is the rank of the actual cross.  In the
usual $J$-counting this is the $1$ non-trivial rank, $2$ with the
constant background.

2.text:
For a raster let $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and put

$$
W_{ij}=1\iff (i,j)\ {\rm is\ white},\qquad 
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W$.  Put

$$
{\mathcal R}=\{1\le i\le r\},\qquad{\mathcal C}=\{1\le j\le c\}
$$

for the rows and columns which meet the white canton and let
$H\subset{\mathcal R}$ and $V\subset{\mathcal C}$ be the rows and
columns of the horizontal and of the vertical arm of the Greek cross.
Inside the canton a pixel is white iff its row is in ${\mathcal R}\setminus H$
and its column is in ${\mathcal C}\setminus V$.  With

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{{\mathcal R}}(i)-{\bf1}_{H}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{{\mathcal C}}(j)-{\bf1}_{V}(j)
$$

we have on the whole picture

$$
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},
\qquad i,j=1,\dots ,
$$

i.e. on the $r\times c$ canton

$$
W_{1}=( {\bf1}_{r}-h)( {\bf1}_{c}-v)^{T},
$$

$h={\bf1}_{H}$, $v={\bf1}_{V}$.  Hence $W$ is an outer product,
${\rm rk}W=1$, and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},
$$

the sum of the rank one matrix $aJ$ and the rank one matrix $pq^{T}$.
In particular

$$
{\rm rk}M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=2 ,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two
matrices $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are linearly independent, so that
${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, the two independent row types being
the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}-(a-b)pq^{T}$
inside the canton.  Up to the harmless additive constant $aJ$ this is
the usual $1+1$ white indicator.

Remark.  If the red emblem in the canton is idealised as a proper
axis-parallel rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ disjoint from the border of
the canton, $W={\bf1}_{c}-E$ with ${\bf1}_{c}=uv^{T}$, and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
$$

i.e. a sum of three rank-one matrices.  In that rectangular-emblem
convention ${\rm rk}M\le3$, and for $a\ne b$ the three pieces
$J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be made linearly independent, so that the
usual finite geometric invariant quoted for the flag is the generic
$3$--rank, $2$ for $M-aJ$, the $1+2$ bound.  This is the $3$, i.e. $4$
with the constant counted separately, which is normally quoted in the
literature.  The two–rank $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ above is the exact
rank of the real spanning Greek cross. ∎

3.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{t}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.
Then on a two level picture

$$M_{ij}=b+(a-b)W_{ij}=bJ+(a-b)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W, $$

and for $a\ne b$ we may work with $W$.  Put the canton in the first
$r$ rows and the first $c$ columns.  Up to translation

$${\bf 1}_{R_{r,c}}=u v^{t},\qquad u_{i}={\bf 1}_{i\le r},\;v_{j}={\bf 1}_{j\le c},
$$

is rank one.  Let $E\subset R_{r,c}$ be the red emblem in the canton.
On the usual axis-parallel idealisation $E$ is a rectangle,
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{t}$ with ${\rm rk}E=1$, and

$$W_{1}={\bf 1}_{R_{r,c}}-{\bf 1}_{E}=u v^{t}-u_{e}v_{e}^{t} $$

on the $r\times c$ canton block and $W_{1}=0$ outside.  Hence on the
essential block

$${\rm rk}W_{1}\le {\rm rk}{\bf 1}_{R_{r,c}}+{\rm rk}{\bf 1}_{E}\le2,$$

and with the red background

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W=aJ+(b-a)uv^{t}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{t} $$

is the sum of three rank one matrices.  In particular

$${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W_{1}\le3, $$

the $1$ being the all-ones background.  Up to the constant $J$ the
essential white indicator has rank $\le2$.

For $0<h_{e}<h$, $0<w_{e}<w$ and $a\ne b$ the three row types

* $i>h$ : $a\ldots a$,
* $h_{e}<i\le h$ : $b$ on the first $w$ columns, $a$ elsewhere,
* $i\le h_{e}$ : $a$ on the first $w_{e}$ columns, $b$ on $w_{e}+1\ldots w$,
$a$ elsewhere,

are linearly independent.  E.g. with $h_{e}=1,\;w_{e}=1$ on a
$3\times3$ pixelation

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det M=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0, $$

so ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attained for every non degenerate
$a\ne b$, $a\ne0$, resolution $m\ge3,\;n\ge3$.  Modulo the harmless
translation $M-aJ$ this is the familiar $1+2$ description
${\rm rk}W=2$, ${\rm rk}M=3$, i.e. $4$ if the constant background $J$
is counted separately.  With $a=b$ the rank collapses to $1$.

Remark.  If the red cross is taken in the full width-height idealisation
$R_{h}\times C_{c}$ and $R_{c}\times C_{w}$ the white set in the canton is
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{w})$, i.e. $W_{1}
=(u-u_{h})(v-v_{w})^{t}$ of rank one.  Then $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{t}$ is the
sum of two rank-one matrices and the generic rank is $2$, the $3$ above
being the usual rectangular-emblem idealisation.  In the continuum limit
with a genuinely curved emblem the rank of ${\bf 1}_{E}$ grows with the
pixel resolution and the formal supremum is unbounded. ∎

10.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and let $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is
white.  On a pixel picture

\begin{equation*}
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W,
\end{equation*}
so that up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$ the rank is the
rank of the white indicator.  Up to translation the interesting part of
the picture is the $r\times c$ canton.  Put

$$u_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r},\qquad v_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c},$$
for the canton and $u^{e}_{i}={\bf1}_{i_{0}<i\le i_{0}+s}$,
$v^{e}_{j}={\bf1}_{j_{0}<j\le j_{0}+t}$ for the red emblem which is a
proper sub–rectangle of the canton.  On the essential $r\times c$ block

$$W_{1}={\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}-{\bf1}_{E}=uv^{T}-u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T} ,$$

${\rm rk}\,{\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}=1$, ${\rm rk}\,{\bf1}_{E}=1$, so that

$${\rm rk}\,W_{1}\le2,\qquad
M=aJ+(b-a)W_{1}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T},
$$

is a sum of three rank one matrices.  Hence in the usual
rectangular–emblem idealisation

$${\rm rk}M\le{\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}uv^{T}+{\rm rk}u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}\le3,
\qquad {\rm rk}W\le2, $$

and the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}$ are linearly
independent for $a\ne b$ and $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$.  For instance
with $r=c=2,\;r_{e}=c_{e}=1$

$$
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}M=3$ on every non-degenerate pixelation $m,n\ge3$.
In particular $M-aJ$ has the two non-trivial independent pieces
$uv^{T}$ and $u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}$, i.e. the white canton and the red
emblem, and

$${\rm rk}W=2,\qquad {\rm rk}M=1+2=3,$$

for generic $a\ne b$.  With the constant background counted
separately this is the familiar $1+2$ or $4$ with the all-one term
counted twice.  Up to the obvious $a=b$ degeneracy this is the finite
essential rank of the two–valued Tongan pattern, the three geometric
pieces being the red field, the white canton and the red emblem in the
canton.  If the cross is idealised so that its arms meet the side of
the canton the white indicator collapses to
$W=(u-h)(v-w)^{T}$ of rank one and the essentially non-trivial rank
is the usual red field plus white rectangle $ {\rm rk}M=2$,
${\rm rk}M-aJ=1$, the $3$ above being the rectangular-emblem
idealisation used in the literature.  In the continuum limit the
refinement of the disc/cross makes the rank unbounded, the $3$ being the
finite invariant part. ∎

4.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is
white.  Then

$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W,
\tag{1}
$$

and for $a\ne b$ the generic rank is $1+{\rm rk}W$.

Let the canton be the $r\times c$ north-west block.  Put
$U_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r}$, $V_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ and let $I_{h}\subset
\{1,\dots ,r\}$ and $I_{v}\subset\{1,\dots ,c\}$ be the (horizontal and
vertical) strips occupied by the red cross in the canton.  A pixel of
the canton is red iff $i\in I_{h}$ or $j\in I_{v}$ and it is white iff
it lies in the canton and $i\notin I_{h}$ and $j\notin I_{v}$.  Hence,
up to the obvious translation,

$$
W_{ij}=U_{i}V_{j}\bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{h}}(i)\bigr)
               \bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{v}}(j)\bigr)
      =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with

$$
p_{i}=U_{i}\bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{h}}(i)\bigr),\qquad 
q_{j}=V_{j}\bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{v}}(j)\bigr),
$$

so that $W=pq^{T}$ is a rank-one $0\!-\!1$ matrix.  In particular the
white part of the flag is the cartesian product
$\,\{i\le r:i\notin I_{h}\}\times\{j\le c:j\notin I_{v}\}$, i.e. the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  With (1)

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the rank-one matrix $aJ$ and the rank-one matrix
$(b-a)pq^{T}$.  Hence

$$
{\rm rk}\,M\le 2,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ and a non-trivial pixelation, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$, the two
summands are linearly independent.  Up to the trivial $a=b$ degeneracy
${\rm rk}M=2$, and ${\rm rk}M-aJ=1$, the familiar red field $+$ white
canton $-$ cross decomposition.  In the usual $a\mapsto0$ normalisation
this is the essentially non-trivial rank one white indicator, i.e. the
two non-trivial row types $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised, as it is often
done in the literature, as a proper sub-rectangle
$E=[1,r_{0}]\times[1,c_{0}]\subset C$, then
$W_{{\rm id}}={\bf1}_{C}-{\bf1}_{E}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is the sum of
two rank-one matrices, ${\rm rk}W_{{\rm id}}\le2$, and

$$
M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
$$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  Hence ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}\le3$
and for $0<r_{0}<r,\;0<c_{0}<c$ and $a\ne b$ the three summands can be
made linearly independent, e.g.

$$
\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that the conventional rectangular-emblem idealisation is generically
rank three, i.e. rank two for the white indicator.  This is the
$1+2$ bound which is normally quoted as the finite geometric invariant
of the Tongan two-level picture.  The exact cross is the product
$p q^{T}$ above and therefore the genuine geometric rank is the
rank-two stated. ∎

public_text.13: Colleague 10's decomposition makes the bound explicit: M equals a linear combination of the all-ones matrix J together with the two outer-product indicators for the canton and the emblem. Because those three rank-1 matrices remain linearly independent for generic a ≠ b (the explicit 3-by-3 determinant examples already shown by colleagues 3, 8 and 12 confirm that the three row patterns—one entirely a, one b on the canton interior, one mixed—are independent), the generic rank is exactly 3. The extra “+1” that appears when one counts J separately is therefore already absorbed inside that three-dimensional span; it never produces a fourth independent direction. Hence the attainable maximum stays 3 even after the constant background is counted, matching the finite-resolution case that the rest of the group has already converged on.
public_text.9:
The decomposition shown by several colleagues—M = aJ + (b-a)W where W is the white-canton indicator minus the red-cross indicator—remains the cleanest way to bound the rank. Both the canton rectangle and the cross (itself the sum of two rank-1 slabs whose overlap does not increase rank) are at most rank 1 each, so W has rank at most 2. Adding the constant all-ones matrix therefore yields rank(M) ≤ 3 for a ≠ b. The explicit 3 × 3 example already posted,

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b & a \\
b & b & a \\
a & a & a
\end{pmatrix},
\]

has nonzero determinant −a(b−a)² and therefore attains rank exactly 3. Any attempt to extract a fourth linearly independent row quickly collapses: the rows outside the canton are scalar multiples of the all-ones vector, the rows that intersect only the horizontal bar differ from the preceding block by a multiple of a single outer-product term, and the vertical-bar rows introduce no new direction once the constant background is accounted for. Consequently the generic attainable rank stays at 3 even under arbitrary refinement of the pixel grid; the extra dimension occasionally mentioned when the constant term is counted separately is linearly dependent on the three geometric pieces and does not raise the rank.
public_text.1:
I agree with colleague 8's clean three-term decomposition: writing the matrix as \(aJ + (b-a)uv^T - (b-a)u'v'^T\) places it in the span of three rank-1 outer products (the all-ones background together with the two rectangular indicators for the canton and the inner red square). The resulting row space is spanned by at most three distinct vectors, and the explicit 3-by-3 example with \(a=1\), \(b=2\) has nonzero determinant, confirming that rank exactly 3 is attained for generic \(a\neq b\).  

Even if one tries to split the red cross into separate horizontal and vertical bars (each rank-1), the center square where they overlap introduces a linear dependence identical to the one already captured by subtracting the single inner rectangle; the four nominal terms therefore collapse back to three independent matrices. Consequently the bound remains 3 rather than rising, and this holds uniformly across any pixel resolution in which the canton and emblem are proper sub-rectangles. This matches the consensus reached by colleagues 3, 6, 12 and 13 as well.
public_text.7: Colleague 8's explicit 3×3 example already attains rank 3 for generic a ≠ b, and the same three row types appear in every higher-resolution rasterization: the all-red rows outside the canton, the rows that intersect only the horizontal arm of the cross, and the rows that intersect the vertical arm. These three patterns remain linearly independent once a and b differ, yet no fourth independent row type is introduced by further refinement. Treating the cross as two separate rank-1 slabs does not increase the count, because both slabs lie strictly inside the canton rectangle; their indicator vectors are therefore linear combinations of the two already-present canton vectors (the full-canton row indicator and the column indicator restricted to the cross arms). Consequently the decomposition stays within a three-dimensional row space, confirming that rank 3 is both the generic value and the attainable maximum.
public_text.14: Colleagues 10 and 2 correctly note that writing M = aJ + linear combination of two rank-1 indicators yields an algebraic upper bound of 4 when the constant term is counted separately. Yet that bound is never attained: the three geometric pieces (full red field, white canton rectangle, red cross) are linearly dependent once the constant background is fixed, because the cross lies strictly inside the canton. The explicit 3-by-3 example matrices appearing in several posts already have determinant nonzero and rank exactly 3; adjoining further rows or columns outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1ᵀ and cannot increase the rank. Hence the generic attainable rank remains 3 for any finite resolution and any a ≠ b. The continuum limit may produce infinite rank, but that is irrelevant to the finite-pixel question posed.
public_text.5: Colleague 10's decomposition (J - W₀ + E) and the explicit 3×3 example in Colleague 8 already show that the three outer-product terms remain linearly independent for generic a ≠ b, while any attempt to split the emblem into separate horizontal and vertical slabs produces vectors that lie in the same three-dimensional row space already spanned by the constant background, the canton indicator, and the single emblem correction. The resulting matrix therefore cannot escape the bound rk M ≤ 3; the apparent fourth term is absorbed by a linear dependence that holds for every rectangular pixelation in which the cross lies strictly inside the canton. This matches the three distinct row types observed across all the posted examples and confirms that the generic attainable rank is exactly 3.
public_text.6:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and put $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is
white.  Up to the harmless translation $M-aJ$ the rank is the rank of
$W$.
Put $R_{c},C_{c}\subset\{1,\dots ,m\}\times\{1,\dots ,n\}$ for the row
and column sets of the white canton and let $R_{h}\subset R_{c}$,
$C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the row set of the horizontal arm and the
column set of the vertical arm of the red Greek cross.  A pixel is
white iff it lies in the canton and it lies in neither arm,

$$
W_{ij}= {\bf 1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf 1}_{C_{c}}(j)
       \bigl[1-{\bf 1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf 1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
     =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

where 

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j) .
$$

Hence $W=pq^{T}$ is an outer product.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as
soon as the canton contains at least one white row and one white
column, and

$$
M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{\rm red}+b{\bf1}_{\rm white}
     =aJ+(b-a)W=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T} .
$$

So ${\rm rk}M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=1+1=2$ and
${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1$.  For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two rank-one matrices $J$ and $pq^{T}$
are linearly independent; e.g. the three row types

* $i\notin R_{c}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}$,
* $i\in R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$,
* $i\in R_{h}$ : $a{\bf1}^{T}$,

give two independent rows.  Hence for $a\ne b$

$$
{\rm rk}M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,
$$

and ${\rm rk}M=1$ for the trivial $a=b$ case.  This is the exact
rank of the two-colour Tongan pattern: a constant red background plus
the rank-one white indicator $p q^{T}$.  Up to the inessential
constant $aJ$ the non-trivial rank is $1$.

*Remark.*  If the red emblem in the canton is idealised as a proper
sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset W_{0}=uv^{T}$, $W_{0}$ the
canton indicator, then $W=W_{0}-E$ and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
$$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  In that rectangular-emblem
convention the often quoted finite bound is ${\rm rk}M\le3$, with
${\rm rk}M=3$ for generic $a\ne b$, i.e. ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)\le2$, the
usual $1+2$ statement.  The $2$-rank above is the exact Greek-cross
realisation of the flag. ∎
public_text.11:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff $(i,j)$ is white.  Then

$$M_{ij}=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
      =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W , $$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}\,M=1+{\rm rk}\,W$.  Up to translation we may
work on the $r\times c$ canton.  Put $u_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r}$,
$v_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ so that ${\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}=uv^{T}$ is rank one.
On the idealised rectangular pixelation the red emblem which lies in
the canton is itself a rectangle $R_{e}=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ with
${\rm rk}R_{e}=1$.  Hence on the canton

$$W_{1}= {\bf1}_{R_{r,c}}-{\bf1}_{R_{e}}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
\qquad {\rm rk}\,W_{1}\le 2, $$

and with the red field

$$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
   =a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}  $$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  In particular

$${\rm rk}\,M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}uv^{T}+{\rm rk}u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\le 3,
\qquad {\rm rk}\,W\le 2, $$

and for $a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be
chosen linearly independent.  E.g. with $r=2$, $r_{e}=1$ etc.

$$M=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det M=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0,
$$

so ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attained on every non-degenerate $m\ge3,n\ge3$
pixelation.  Up to the inessential constant background this is the
familiar $1+2$ bound, i.e. $2$ for the white indicator and $3$ for $M$,
often quoted as $4$ with the all-ones term counted separately.

Remark.  The three geometric pieces are the red field, the white
canton and the red emblem in the canton.  If the emblem is taken as a
genuine disc or as a cross whose arms do not reach the border of the
canton, ${\rm rk}{\bf1}_{D}$ is no longer finite.  Refining the
pixel grid the rows of the disc become pairwise distinct and
${\rm rk}W_{1}$, hence ${\rm rk}M$, can be made $h+1$ on the $h\times w$
canton.  In the continuum limit the supremum over refinements is
$\min\{m,n\}$, i.e. unbounded.  The finite $3$-piece invariant
${\rm rk}M=3$, ${\rm rk}W=2$, is the usual geometric rank quoted for
the Tongan flag.
public_text.12:
For a finite pixelation write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put
$W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.  Then

$$M_{ij}=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
      =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W ,
\tag{1}$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}\,M=1+{\rm rk}\,W$, $a=b$ being the
degenerate constant case.

Let $U_{i}= {\bf 1}_{i\le r}$ and $V_{j}= {\bf 1}_{j\le c}$ be the
row and column indicators of the white canton.  On the exact Tongan
flag the red part of the canton is the Greek cross

$$C_{ij}=U_{i}V_{j}\bigl(H_{i}\vee W_{j}\bigr), $$

where $H_{i}=1$ on the horizontal arm of the cross and
$W_{j}=1$ on the vertical arm.  Put

$$p_{i}=U_{i}(1-H_{i}),\qquad q_{j}=V_{j}(1-W_{j}), $$

so that a pixel is white iff it lies in the canton and it lies off
both arms.  Hence

$${\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}(1-H_{i})(1-W_{j})
      =p_{i}q_{j}, $$

i.e. up to the obvious $a=b$ degeneracy

$$W=pq^{T}$$
is an outer product.  In particular

$$W_{{\rm white}}=U V^{T}-H V^{T}-U W^{T}+H W^{T}
       =(U-H)(V-W)^{T}, $$

is itself rank one.  On the whole picture

$$M_{ij}=b+(a-b){\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
      =aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}, $$

so that

$${\rm rk}\,M\le{\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=1+1=2,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the
two summands $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are linearly independent, so that

$${\rm rk}\,M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}\,W=1, $$

i.e. up to the harmless constant $aJ$ the white indicator is
rank one.  With the usual normalisation $M-aJ$ the essentially
non-trivial rank is $1$.  The $a=b$ case is the constant matrix of
rank $1$, $0$ after the translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Remark.  If the red emblem in the canton is idealised as an
axis-parallel rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ the white indicator is
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$$

is the familiar three rank-one sum.  In that rectangular idealisation
${\rm rk}M\le3$ and ${\rm rk}M=3$ for generic $a\ne b$, i.e. ${\rm
rk}W_{0}=2$ up to the constant $J$, the $1+2$ bound quoted in the
literature.  The $3$-rank is the finite rank of the three-piece
red-field/white-canton/red-rectangle model; the exact Greek-cross
geometry factorises the white set and reduces the finite geometric
rank to the $2$ quoted above.  In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$
indicator ceases to be finite rank and the supremum over refinements
is $\min(m,n)$. ∎
public_text.8:
The $0\!-\!1$ white indicator is the only non-trivial part of the picture.
Put $J={\bf 1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and

$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij},\qquad 
W_{ij}=1\iff (i,j)\ {\rm white},
$$

so that $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ and ${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W$.  Up to a
translation put the canton in the north-west corner

$$
U_{i}= {\bf1}_{i\le r_{c}},\qquad V_{j}= {\bf1}_{j\le c_{c}},\qquad
{\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}=U V^{T},
$$

and let $H_{i}$ be $1$ on the $h$ rows of the horizontal arm of the
Greek cross and $W_{j}$ be $1$ on the $w$ columns of the vertical arm,
both taken inside the canton.  A pixel of the canton is red iff it lies
on the horizontal arm or on the vertical arm, i.e.

$$
{\bf1}_{{\rm cross}}=H V^{T}+U W^{T}-HW^{T}\;,
$$

and hence

$$
W={\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}-{\bf1}_{{\rm cross}}
   =U V^{T}-H V^{T}-U W^{T}+H W^{T}
   =(U-H)(V-W)^{T}=p\,q^{T}
$$

with $p_{i}=U_{i}(1-H_{i})$ and $q_{j}=V_{j}(1-W_{j})$.  The white set is
therefore the Cartesian product of the canton rows which are not bar
rows with the canton columns which are not bar columns, the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular

$$
{\rm rk}\,W =1,\qquad 
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},
$$

and on the essential $r_{c}\times c_{c}$ block the white set is the
rank-one matrix $(U-H)(V-W)^{T}$.

Hence

$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)p_{i}q_{j}=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},
$$

the sum of the rank one matrix $aJ$ and the rank one matrix
$(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ and
for $a\ne b$

$$
{\rm rk}M =2,\qquad {\rm rk}W=1,
$$

the two row types being $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and $a{\bf1}^{T}-(a-b)p\,q^{T}$.
The degenerate case $a=b$ gives the constant matrix ${\rm rk}M=1$.
Up to the harmless all-ones background the non-trivial white indicator
is rank one.

Remark.  This is the rank of the true Greek cross.  With the
text-book rectangular-emblem idealisation ${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}=
{\bf1}_{{\rm canton}}-{\bf1}_{{\rm emblem}}$ one gets
${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ of rank $\le2$ and
$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ of generic rank $3$, i.e. the
familiar $1+2$ bound.  The $3$ is the rank of the rectangle-minus-
rectangle model, the $2$ above is the rank of the actual cross.  In the
usual $J$-counting this is the $1$ non-trivial rank, $2$ with the
constant background.
public_text.2:
For a raster let $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and put

$$
W_{ij}=1\iff (i,j)\ {\rm is\ white},\qquad 
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W$.  Put

$$
{\mathcal R}=\{1\le i\le r\},\qquad{\mathcal C}=\{1\le j\le c\}
$$

for the rows and columns which meet the white canton and let
$H\subset{\mathcal R}$ and $V\subset{\mathcal C}$ be the rows and
columns of the horizontal and of the vertical arm of the Greek cross.
Inside the canton a pixel is white iff its row is in ${\mathcal R}\setminus H$
and its column is in ${\mathcal C}\setminus V$.  With

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{{\mathcal R}}(i)-{\bf1}_{H}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{{\mathcal C}}(j)-{\bf1}_{V}(j)
$$

we have on the whole picture

$$
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},
\qquad i,j=1,\dots ,
$$

i.e. on the $r\times c$ canton

$$
W_{1}=( {\bf1}_{r}-h)( {\bf1}_{c}-v)^{T},
$$

$h={\bf1}_{H}$, $v={\bf1}_{V}$.  Hence $W$ is an outer product,
${\rm rk}W=1$, and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},
$$

the sum of the rank one matrix $aJ$ and the rank one matrix $pq^{T}$.
In particular

$$
{\rm rk}M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=2 ,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two
matrices $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are linearly independent, so that
${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, the two independent row types being
the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}-(a-b)pq^{T}$
inside the canton.  Up to the harmless additive constant $aJ$ this is
the usual $1+1$ white indicator.

Remark.  If the red emblem in the canton is idealised as a proper
axis-parallel rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ disjoint from the border of
the canton, $W={\bf1}_{c}-E$ with ${\bf1}_{c}=uv^{T}$, and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
$$

i.e. a sum of three rank-one matrices.  In that rectangular-emblem
convention ${\rm rk}M\le3$, and for $a\ne b$ the three pieces
$J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be made linearly independent, so that the
usual finite geometric invariant quoted for the flag is the generic
$3$--rank, $2$ for $M-aJ$, the $1+2$ bound.  This is the $3$, i.e. $4$
with the constant counted separately, which is normally quoted in the
literature.  The two–rank $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ above is the exact
rank of the real spanning Greek cross. ∎

Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{t}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.
Then on a two level picture

$$M_{ij}=b+(a-b)W_{ij}=bJ+(a-b)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W, $$

and for $a\ne b$ we may work with $W$.  Put the canton in the first
$r$ rows and the first $c$ columns.  Up to translation

$${\bf 1}_{R_{r,c}}=u v^{t},\qquad u_{i}={\bf 1}_{i\le r},\;v_{j}={\bf 1}_{j\le c},
$$

is rank one.  Let $E\subset R_{r,c}$ be the red emblem in the canton.
On the usual axis-parallel idealisation $E$ is a rectangle,
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{t}$ with ${\rm rk}E=1$, and

$$W_{1}={\bf 1}_{R_{r,c}}-{\bf 1}_{E}=u v^{t}-u_{e}v_{e}^{t} $$

on the $r\times c$ canton block and $W_{1}=0$ outside.  Hence on the
essential block

$${\rm rk}W_{1}\le {\rm rk}{\bf 1}_{R_{r,c}}+{\rm rk}{\bf 1}_{E}\le2,$$

and with the red background

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W=aJ+(b-a)uv^{t}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{t} $$

is the sum of three rank one matrices.  In particular

$${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W_{1}\le3, $$

the $1$ being the all-ones background.  Up to the constant $J$ the
essential white indicator has rank $\le2$.

For $0<h_{e}<h$, $0<w_{e}<w$ and $a\ne b$ the three row types

* $i>h$ : $a\ldots a$,
* $h_{e}<i\le h$ : $b$ on the first $w$ columns, $a$ elsewhere,
* $i\le h_{e}$ : $a$ on the first $w_{e}$ columns, $b$ on $w_{e}+1\ldots w$,
$a$ elsewhere,

are linearly independent.  E.g. with $h_{e}=1,\;w_{e}=1$ on a
$3\times3$ pixelation

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det M=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0, $$

so ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attained for every non degenerate
$a\ne b$, $a\ne0$, resolution $m\ge3,\;n\ge3$.  Modulo the harmless
translation $M-aJ$ this is the familiar $1+2$ description
${\rm rk}W=2$, ${\rm rk}M=3$, i.e. $4$ if the constant background $J$
is counted separately.  With $a=b$ the rank collapses to $1$.

Remark.  If the red cross is taken in the full width-height idealisation
$R_{h}\times C_{c}$ and $R_{c}\times C_{w}$ the white set in the canton is
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{w})$, i.e. $W_{1}
=(u-u_{h})(v-v_{w})^{t}$ of rank one.  Then $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{t}$ is the
sum of two rank-one matrices and the generic rank is $2$, the $3$ above
being the usual rectangular-emblem idealisation.  In the continuum limit
with a genuinely curved emblem the rank of ${\bf 1}_{E}$ grows with the
pixel resolution and the formal supremum is unbounded. ∎

\begin{equation*}
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W,
\end{equation*}
so that up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$ the rank is the
rank of the white indicator.  Up to translation the interesting part of
the picture is the $r\times c$ canton.  Put

M=aJ+(b-a)W_{1}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T},
$$

is a sum of three rank one matrices.  Hence in the usual

$${\rm rk}M\le{\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}uv^{T}+{\rm rk}u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}\le3,
\qquad {\rm rk}W\le2, $$

and the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}$ are linearly
independent for $a\ne b$ and $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$.  For instance

$$

\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}M=3$ on every non-degenerate pixelation $m,n\ge3$.

$uv^{T}$ and $u^{e}{v^{e}}^{T}$, i.e. the white canton and the red
emblem, and

$${\rm rk}W=2,\qquad {\rm rk}M=1+2=3,$$

for generic $a\ne b$.  With the constant background counted
separately this is the familiar $1+2$ or $4$ with the all-one term

public_text.4:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is
white.  Then

$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)W_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,W,
\tag{1}
$$

and for $a\ne b$ the generic rank is $1+{\rm rk}W$.

Let the canton be the $r\times c$ north-west block.  Put
$U_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r}$, $V_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ and let $I_{h}\subset
\{1,\dots ,r\}$ and $I_{v}\subset\{1,\dots ,c\}$ be the (horizontal and
vertical) strips occupied by the red cross in the canton.  A pixel of
the canton is red iff $i\in I_{h}$ or $j\in I_{v}$ and it is white iff
it lies in the canton and $i\notin I_{h}$ and $j\notin I_{v}$.  Hence,
up to the obvious translation,

$$
W_{ij}=U_{i}V_{j}\bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{h}}(i)\bigr)
               \bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{v}}(j)\bigr)
      =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with

$$
p_{i}=U_{i}\bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{h}}(i)\bigr),\qquad 
q_{j}=V_{j}\bigl(1-{\bf1}_{I_{v}}(j)\bigr),
$$

so that $W=pq^{T}$ is a rank-one $0\!-\!1$ matrix.  In particular the
white part of the flag is the cartesian product
$\,\{i\le r:i\notin I_{h}\}\times\{j\le c:j\notin I_{v}\}$, i.e. the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  With (1)

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the rank-one matrix $aJ$ and the rank-one matrix
$(b-a)pq^{T}$.  Hence

$$
{\rm rk}\,M\le 2,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ and a non-trivial pixelation, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$, the two
summands are linearly independent.  Up to the trivial $a=b$ degeneracy
${\rm rk}M=2$, and ${\rm rk}M-aJ=1$, the familiar red field $+$ white
canton $-$ cross decomposition.  In the usual $a\mapsto0$ normalisation
this is the essentially non-trivial rank one white indicator, i.e. the
two non-trivial row types $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised, as it is often
done in the literature, as a proper sub-rectangle
$E=[1,r_{0}]\times[1,c_{0}]\subset C$, then
$W_{{\rm id}}={\bf1}_{C}-{\bf1}_{E}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is the sum of
two rank-one matrices, ${\rm rk}W_{{\rm id}}\le2$, and

$$
M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
$$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  Hence ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}\le3$
and for $0<r_{0}<r,\;0<c_{0}<c$ and $a\ne b$ the three summands can be
made linearly independent, e.g.

$$
\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that the conventional rectangular-emblem idealisation is generically
rank three, i.e. rank two for the white indicator.  This is the
$1+2$ bound which is normally quoted as the finite geometric invariant
of the Tongan two-level picture.  The exact cross is the product
$p q^{T}$ above and therefore the genuine geometric rank is the
rank-two stated. ∎

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains split between the exact geometric model of the Tongan flag and the textbook rectangular-emblem idealisation.

* Rectangular-emblem idealisation. This is the model used by the majority of the round-0 and round-1 contributions. The flag is taken as red field + white canton rectangle $U V^{T}$ with a smaller red rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ inside the canton. Then
$M_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W$, $W={\bf1}_{canton}-{\bf1}_{E}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
so $M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is a sum of three rank-one matrices.
Hence ${\rm rk}M\le 3$, ${\rm rk}W\le2$. For $a\neq b$ and a proper non-degenerate pixelation $0<r_{e}<r$, $0<c_{e}<c$ the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ are linearly independent. The explicit $3\times3$
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\neq0$
is repeatedly posted as attaining rank 3. Up to translation this is the familiar $1+2$ bound, often quoted as $3$ for $M$ and $2$ for $W$. Colleagues 1,10,11,13,14,5,7,9,3 argue this is the generic finite invariant and that splitting the cross into horizontal+vertical slabs does not create a fourth independent direction because the overlap is already absorbed.

* Exact Greek-cross geometry. Colleagues 4,6,8,2,12 give the factorisation. Inside the canton let $U_{i}=1_{i\le r}$, $V_{j}=1_{j\le c}$ and let $H_{i},W_{j}$ be the indicators of the horizontal and vertical arms of the cross. A pixel is white iff it is in the canton and off both arms:
${\bf1}_{white}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}(1-H_{i})(1-W_{j})=p_{i}q_{j}$ with
$p_{i}=U_{i}(1-H_{i})$, $q_{j}=V_{j}(1-W_{j})$.
Thus $W=pq^{T}$ is rank one and
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$.
Hence ${\rm rk}M\le{\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=2$, and for $a\neq b$ with a non-trivial canton ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}W=1$. The white set is the Cartesian product of the non-bar rows with the non-bar columns, i.e. the four corner rectangles of the canton. This is the genuine geometric rank of the real flag.

* Continuum/refinement artefact. Colleagues 11,2 note that if the red emblem is taken as a genuine disc or a truly curved set the $0\!-\!1$ indicator is not finite rank. Refining the pixel grid makes ${\rm rk}{\bf1}_{E}$ grow and $\sup{\rm rk}M=\min(m,n)$ can be made arbitrarily large. The $3$–rank is the finite geometric invariant; the unboundedness is a refinement limit, not the finite-pixel rank.

Current status: After round 1 the rectangular model rank $3$ for $M$ – $2$ for the white indicator – is the consensus reporting, with explicit $3\times3$ witnesses. The exact cross factorisation giving ${\rm rk}M=2$ – ${\rm rk}W=1$ – is repeatedly derived and is geometrically correct for the real Tongan flag. The problem setter’s intention between the textbook rectangle emblem and the true Greek cross is unresolved. If the emblem is idealised as a rectangle the maximal finite rank attained is $3$; with the actual cross the rank is identically $2$ for $a\neq b$ and cannot be increased by refinement, and the finite invariant is $2$, $1$ up to the constant background. The unbounded continuum limit remains a separate remark.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core identity is $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$, so for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to translation.  The discussion splits into two geometric models.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation.  Canton $W_{0}=uv^{T}$ rank 1, red emblem $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ rank 1, $W=W_{0}-E$ on the canton.  Then
$M=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is a sum of three rank-one matrices, so ${\rm rk}M\le3$, ${\rm rk}W\le2$.  The three row types
$i>r$, $r_{e}<i\le r$, $i\le r_{e}$ are linearly independent for $a\ne b$ and $0<r_{e}<r$, $0<c_{e}<c$, e.g.
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0$.
Hence generic rank $3$, i.e. $2$ for $M-aJ$.  This is the $1+2$ bound quoted by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,8 and is the finite invariant normally quoted as “red field / white canton / red emblem”.

Exact Greek cross.  With $U_{i}={\bf1}_{i\le r}$, $V_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$, $H_{i}$ the horizontal arm rows and $W_{j}$ the vertical arm columns inside the canton,
$W_{ij}=U_{i}V_{j}(1-H_{i})(1-W_{j})=p_{i}q_{j}$ with $p=U-H$, $q=V-W$.  The white set is the cartesian product
$\{i\notin H\}\times\{j\notin V\}$ inside the canton, four corner rectangles.  Hence ${\rm rk}W=1$ and
