The supremum over refinements is unbounded only for a genuinely curved emblem, e.g. a disc, which is not the Tongan cross. With the real flag the rank is resolution independent, maximal $2$ for $a\ne b$, $1$ for $a=b$, i.e. $1$ up to the harmless constant $aJ$.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The matrix is $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^T$, so ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$ and for $a\ne b$ generically ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$.
The white indicator controls the rank.

Exact Greek-cross geometry. Canton $R_c\times C_c$. Horizontal arm $R_h\subset R_c$, vertical arm $C_v\subset C_c$. A pixel is white iff $i\in R_c\setminus R_h$ and $j\in C_c\setminus C_v$. Hence
$W_{ij}=p_iq_j$ with $p_i={\bf1}_{R_c\setminus R_h}(i)$, $q_j={\bf1}_{C_c\setminus C_v}(j)$.
$W=pq^T$ is rank one as soon as the canton contains a white row and column. Then
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^T$ is sum of two rank-one matrices, ${\rm rk}M\le2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}M=1$ if $a=b$. This is the exact finite geometric rank of the real spanning cross; the white set is the Cartesian product of the four corner rectangles.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation, the textbook model. Canton ${\bf1}_C=uv^T$ rank one. Red emblem idealised as a proper sub-rectangle $E=u_ev_e^T\subset{\bf1}_C$ rank one. Then
$W_{\rm id}=uv^T-u_ev_e^T$, ${\rm rk}W_{\rm id}\le2$, and
$M_{\rm id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^T-(b-a)u_ev_e^T$
is sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}M_{\rm id}\le3$, ${\rm rk}W_{\rm id}\le2$, and for $0<r_e<r$, $0<c_e<c$, $a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^T,u_ev_e^T$ are generically independent. The $3\times3$ example
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=-(a-b)^2a\neq0$ shows ${\rm rk}M=3$ is attained. Up to translation ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=2$. This is the $1+2$ finite invariant quoted in the literature.

Disagreement / ambiguity. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14,3,6,8,9 defend the rectangular-emblem $3$-rank as the intended maximal finite rank, noting that splitting the cross into horizontal+vertical slabs does not create a fourth independent direction because the overlap is already absorbed in $uv^T-u_ev_e^T$, and adjoining rows outside the canton only repeats the constant row $a{\bf1}^T$. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,8 give the exact Greek-cross factorisation $W=pq^T$ and state the exact rank is $2$, $1$ up to the constant, while remarking that the $3$ is the rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation.

Unbounded refinement. Refining the pixel grid makes the $0\!-\!1$ indicator of a genuine curved/disc emblem have arbitrarily large rank, so $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min\{m,n\}$. The $2$ or $3$ values are the essential finite geometric invariants; the supremum over resolutions is unbounded.

Current standing: exact geometry $\Rightarrow$ generic ${\rm rk}M=2$ [$1$ up to $aJ$]; conventional rectangular-emblem idealisation $\Rightarrow$ generic maximal finite ${\rm rk}M=3$ [$2$ up to $aJ$]. The deliberation consensus quoted in round 0/1 is the $3$-rank idealisation, with the exact cross $2$-rank noted as the precise geometric value.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two-level picture can be written up to translation as
$M=aJ+(b-a)W$, $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$, so for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$.
The white part is the white canton minus the red emblem inside it.

*Rectangular-emblem idealisation.*  Canton $uv^{T}$ rank 1, emblem $u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ rank 1.  
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$.  
$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is sum of three rank-1 matrices, 
${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$, ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)\le2$.  
For $0<h_{e}<h$, $0<w_{e}<w$, $a\ne b$ the three row types
$i>h$, $h_{e}<i\le h$, $i\le h_{e}$ are independent. E.g.
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\neq0$.
Hence generic ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$. This is the $1+2$ finite
invariant quoted in the literature; the $4$ counting $J$ separately collapses
to the three independent directions $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$.

*Exact Greek cross.*  Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be canton rows/columns and $H\subset R_{c}$,
$V\subset C_{c}$ the horizontal and vertical arms. A pixel is white iff
$i\in R_{c}\setminus H$ and $j\in C_{c}\setminus V$:
${\bf1}_{white}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}(1-{\bf1}_{H})(1-{\bf1}_{V})=p_{i}q_{j}$,
$p=U(1-H)$, $q=V(1-V)$. Hence $W=pq^{T}$ rank 1,
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ sum of two rank-1 matrices,
${\rm rk}M\le2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, and ${\rm rk}M=2$ for $a\ne b$ with a
non-trivial pixelation. The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus H)\times(C_{c}\setminus V)$, the four corner rectangles of the
canton.

Current round confirms both statements: colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 give the
exact factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ and ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}W=1$, while noting the
usual rectangular-emblem idealisation gives ${\rm rk}M=3$, ${\rm rk}W=2$.
Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13 argue the four nominal slab indicators collapse to the
same three-dimensional span, so no rank 4 is attainable and the maximal finite
rank under the rectangular model is 3.

Unresolved: which idealisation the question intends. The true Tongan flag has a
spanning Greek cross, so the strict finite geometric rank is 2, i.e. 1 up to the
constant background. The widely quoted textbook invariant is the rectangular-emblem
$3$, i.e. $2$ up to translation. The continuum refinement remark persists:
if the emblem is taken as a genuinely curved set the rank grows with pixel
refinement and $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min\{m,n\}$, i.e. formally unbounded.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The matrix is $M_{ij}=a$ on red, $b$ on white, $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W$ the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator. Up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$ the rank is the rank of $W$ and ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$, with ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ for $a\ne b$.

Put the white canton in the $r\times c$ north-west block, $U_i={\bf1}_{i\le r}$, $V_j={\bf1}_{j\le c}$. Let $H\subset\{1..r\}$ be the rows of the horizontal arm and $K\subset\{1..c\}$ the columns of the vertical arm of the Greek cross. A pixel of the canton is white iff its row is in the canton and not in $H$ and its column is in the canton and not in $K$,

$$W_{ij}=U_iV_j\bigl[1-{\bf1}_H(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_K(j)\bigr]=p_iq_j,\qquad 
p_i=U_i[1-{\bf1}_H(i)],\;q_j=V_j[1-{\bf1}_K(j)].$$

Hence on the whole picture $W=pq^{T}$ is an outer product. The white set is the Cartesian product $(R_c\setminus R_h)\times(C_c\setminus C_v)$, the four corner rectangles of the canton. So ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},$$

the sum of two rank-one matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two summands are independent, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, the two row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the canton rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$. For $a=b$, $M$ is constant, rank $1$ $0$ after translation. This is the exact spanning Greek-cross rank, Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,8.

The often quoted $1+2$ / $3$ bound comes from the textbook rectangular-emblem idealisation. There the red part of the canton is idealised as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_e v_e^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ with $uv^{T}$ the indicator of the canton. Then

$$W_0=uv^{T}-u_e v_e^{T},\qquad M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_e v_e^{T},$$

a sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}W_0\le2$, ${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$, and for $0<r_e<r$, $0<c_e<c$, $a\ne b$ the three pieces $J,uv^{T},u_e v_e^{T}$ can be chosen independent. The familiar $3\times3$ example

$$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det=-(a-b)^2a\ne0,$$

is attained, so generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)=2$. This is the finite invariant quoted by Colleagues 1,3,5,6,7,9,13. The four nominal slab terms for the cross collapse to the same three-dimensional span because the centre square is counted twice, so the “fourth” direction is a linear dependence.

Hence under the exact spanning cross the finite pixel rank is $2$, $1$ up to translation; under the conventional rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation the finite rank is $3$, $2$ up to translation. In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$ indicator ceases to be finite rank and $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min(m,n)$, the unbounded refinement remark made by Colleague 11. The disagreement in round 2 is precisely this exact cross factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ versus the rectangular-emblem model $W_0=uv^{T}-u_e v_e^{T}$.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two-level matrix can be written M = aJ + (b-a)W with J the all-ones matrix and W the 0-1 white indicator. For a≠b rk M =1+rk W up to the harmless translation M→M-aJ.

True Greek-cross geometry. Let the canton be rows R_c, cols C_c and let H⊂R_c be the rows of the horizontal arm and V⊂C_c the columns of the vertical arm. A canton pixel is white iff its row∉H and its column∉V. Hence

1_white(i,j)=1_{R_c}(i)1_{C_c}(j)(1-1_H(i))(1-1_V(j))=p_i q_j

with p_i=1_{R_c\H}(i), q_j=1_{C_c\V}(j). So W=pq^T, rk W=1 as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column, and

M = aJ + (b-a)pq^T

is the sum of two rank-one matrices. For a≠b, p≠0, q≠0 the summands are independent, rk(M-aJ)=1, rk M=2; rk M=1 for the degenerate a=b. The white set is the Cartesian product (R_c\H)×(C_c\V), the four corner rectangles of the canton. This is the exact finite geometric rank of the real spanning cross; no fourth direction appears.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation. The textbook model replaces the cross by a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle E=u_e v_e^T⊂uv^T inside the canton uv^T. Then

W0 = uv^T - u_e v_e^T,   M_id = aJ + (b-a)uv^T - (b-a)u_e v_e^T

is a sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence rk W0≤2, rk M_id≤3 and for 0<r_e<r,0<c_e<c, a≠b the three matrices J,uv^T,u_e v_e^T are generically independent. The 3×3 example

M = [[a,b,a],[b,b,a],[a,a,a]]

has det = -a(b-a)^2≠0, so rk M=3 is attainable. Modulo J this is the familiar 1+2 invariant: rk(M-aJ)=2, rk W0=2, often quoted as rank 3 for M. This is the finite invariant quoted by Colleagues 1,3,8,12,13,14,5,7,9, and is the rank of the red-field/white-canton/red-rectangle model.

Current disagreement. Colleagues 10,11,12,4,2,8 give the exact cross factorisation rk M=2, rk(M-aJ)=1, and explicitly note the 3-rank as the rectangular-emblem idealisation. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 retain the 3-rank as the maximal finite-pixel rank, arguing the four nominal cross slabs collapse to the three independent directions J,uv^T,u_e v_e^T. The “4” counting with the all-ones term counted twice collapses to 3; no construction realising rank 4 has been exhibited.

Unresolved. The problem statement says “the flag of Tonga”. The real flag uses a spanning Greek cross, so the genuine finite geometric rank is 2, i.e. 1 up to the constant background. The rank 3 that dominates the public round is the conventional rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation of the emblem. Continuum/refinement remarks note that in the continuum limit the 0-1 indicator ceases to be finite rank and sup_{m,n} rk M = min(m,n), but this is not finite-pixel.

Working belief remains: exact flag → max rk M=2 for a≠b, rk(M-aJ)=1; the widely quoted textbook finite invariant is rk M=3, rk W=2, i.e. the 1+2 bound. Whether the question intends the idealisation or the true geometry remains the open interpretation.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two-valued matrix can be written as

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T},\qquad W_{ij}=1\iff (i,j)\ {\rm white},$$
so up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$ the rank is $1+{\rm rk}W$ for $a\ne b$.

Exact Greek-cross geometry.  Let $R_c,C_c$ be the rows/columns meeting the canton and $R_h\subset R_c$, $C_v\subset C_c$ the rows/columns of the horizontal and vertical arm.  A canton pixel is white iff it is off both arms,

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_c}(i){\bf1}_{C_c}(j)\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_h}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_v}(j)\bigr]
      =p_iq_j,$$

$$p_i={\bf1}_{R_c\setminus R_h}(i),\qquad q_j={\bf1}_{C_c\setminus C_v}(j).$$

Hence $W=pq^{T}$ is an outer product.  The white set is the Cartesian product $(R_c\setminus R_h)\times(C_c\setminus C_v)$, i.e. the four corner rectangles of the canton.  For a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$,

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},\qquad {\rm rk}W=1,\ {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,$$

and $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are independent for $a\ne b$.  Thus

$${\rm rk}M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,$$

with the degenerate $a=b$ case ${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after translation.  The two independent row types are the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the rows inside the canton $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$.  This is the exact finite geometric rank of the real Tongan red field + white canton – Greek cross, argued in round 2 by Colleagues 10, 11, 12, 4, 2, 8.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation.  The literature often idealises the red emblem in the canton as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_e v_e^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ with $uv^{T}$ the canton indicator.  Then on the $r\times c$ canton

$$W_0=uv^{T}-u_e v_e^{T},\qquad {\rm rk}W_0\le2,$$

and

$$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_e v_e^{T}
      =a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_e v_e^{T}$$

is a sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_e<r,\;0<c_e<c$ and $a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u_e v_e^{T}$ are generically independent, e.g.

$$M_{id}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M_{id}=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0,$$

so ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_0=2$, i.e. ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)=2$.  This is the $1+2$ finite invariant “red field / white canton / red rectangle” quoted by Colleagues 1, 3, 7, 9, 13, 14, 5, and is the bound often stated as rank 3 for $M$, rank 2 for $M-aJ$, sometimes over-counted as $1+2+1=4$.

Disagreement and status.  Round 2 reiterates the split: 10,11,12,4,2,8 keep the exact factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ giving the genuine rank $2$ [$1$ up to translation]; 1,13,14,5,7,9 maintain the textbook rectangular-emblem model giving the attainable finite maximum $3$ [$2$ up to translation].  The discrepancy is precisely the idealisation $E=u_e v_e^{T}$ versus the true full-width/full-height cross $(U-H)(V-W)^{T}$.  No construction escaping the $pq^{T}$ factorisation for the true cross is produced in round 2; the alleged fourth direction collapses because the horizontal and vertical arms lie inside the canton and the centre square is counted twice.

Unresolved quantification.  In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$ indicator ceases to be finite rank and $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min(m,n)$.  For any fixed finite pixelation the exact geometry is rank 2.  The maximal rank quoted in the literature is the rectangular-emblem invariant $3$ for $M$, $2$ for $W$, i.e. $1+2$ up to the constant background.

Current belief: exact flag geometry $\Rightarrow$ maximal finite rank $2$ for $a\ne b$, $1$ for $a=b$, $1$ up to translation.  The conventional $3$-rank statement is the rectangular-emblem idealisation and remains the finite invariant most colleagues cite. ∎

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The persistent identity is $M=aJ+(b-a)W$, $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$, so for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to translation. The discussion is now a split between two geometric models.

Exact spanning Greek cross. Let the canton be $R_{c}\times C_{c}$, $U_{i}=1_{i\le r}$, $V_{j}=1_{j\le c}$ and let $H\subset R_{c}$, $K\subset C_{c}$ be the row set of the horizontal arm and column set of the vertical arm. A pixel in the canton is white iff $i\notin H$, $j\notin K$, i.e.

$W_{ij}=U_{i}V_{j}(1-{\bf1}_{H}(i))(1-{\bf1}_{K}(j))=p_{i}q_{j}$,
$p=U(1-H)$, $q=V(1-K)$. The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\!\setminus\! H)\times(C_{c}\!\setminus\!K)$, the four corner rectangles of the canton. Hence ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and column and

sum of two rank-one matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=1$ for $a=b$. This is argued by Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,8.

${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$, ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)\le2$.  
For $0<h_{e}<h$, $0<w_{e}<w$, $a\ne b$ the three row types
$i>h$, $h_{e}<i\le h$, $i\le h_{e}$ are independent. E.g.
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\neq0$.
Hence generic ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$. This is the $1+2$ finite
invariant quoted in the literature; the $4$ counting $J$ separately collapses
to the three independent directions $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$.

*Exact Greek cross.*  Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be canton rows/columns and $H\subset R_{c}$,
$V\subset C_{c}$ the horizontal and vertical arms. A pixel is white iff
$i\in R_{c}\setminus H$ and $j\in C_{c}\setminus V$:
${\bf1}_{white}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}(1-{\bf1}_{H})(1-{\bf1}_{V})=p_{i}q_{j}$,
$p=U(1-H)$, $q=V(1-V)$. Hence $W=pq^{T}$ rank 1,
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ sum of two rank-1 matrices,
${\rm rk}M\le2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, and ${\rm rk}M=2$ for $a\ne b$ with a
non-trivial pixelation. The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus H)\times(C_{c}\setminus V)$, the four corner rectangles of the
canton.

Current round confirms both statements: colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 give the
exact factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ and ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}W=1$, while noting the
usual rectangular-emblem idealisation gives ${\rm rk}M=3$, ${\rm rk}W=2$.
Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13 argue the four nominal slab indicators collapse to the
same three-dimensional span, so no rank 4 is attainable and the maximal finite
rank under the rectangular model is 3.

reflection_text.6:
The matrix is $M_{ij}=a$ on red, $b$ on white, $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W$ the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator. Up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$ the rank is the rank of $W$ and ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$, with ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ for $a\ne b$.

Put the white canton in the $r\times c$ north-west block, $U_i={\bf1}_{i\le r}$, $V_j={\bf1}_{j\le c}$. Let $H\subset\{1..r\}$ be the rows of the horizontal arm and $K\subset\{1..c\}$ the columns of the vertical arm of the Greek cross. A pixel of the canton is white iff its row is in the canton and not in $H$ and its column is in the canton and not in $K$,

$$W_{ij}=U_iV_j\bigl[1-{\bf1}_H(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_K(j)\bigr]=p_iq_j,\qquad 
p_i=U_i[1-{\bf1}_H(i)],\;q_j=V_j[1-{\bf1}_K(j)].$$

Hence on the whole picture $W=pq^{T}$ is an outer product. The white set is the Cartesian product $(R_c\setminus R_h)\times(C_c\setminus C_v)$, the four corner rectangles of the canton. So ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},$$

the sum of two rank-one matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two summands are independent, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, the two row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the canton rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$. For $a=b$, $M$ is constant, rank $1$ $0$ after translation. This is the exact spanning Greek-cross rank, Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,8.

The often quoted $1+2$ / $3$ bound comes from the textbook rectangular-emblem idealisation. There the red part of the canton is idealised as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_e v_e^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ with $uv^{T}$ the indicator of the canton. Then

$$W_0=uv^{T}-u_e v_e^{T},\qquad M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_e v_e^{T},$$

a sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}W_0\le2$, ${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$, and for $0<r_e<r$, $0<c_e<c$, $a\ne b$ the three pieces $J,uv^{T},u_e v_e^{T}$ can be chosen independent. The familiar $3\times3$ example

$$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det=-(a-b)^2a\ne0,$$

is attained, so generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)=2$. This is the finite invariant quoted by Colleagues 1,3,5,6,7,9,13. The four nominal slab terms for the cross collapse to the same three-dimensional span because the centre square is counted twice, so the “fourth” direction is a linear dependence.

Hence under the exact spanning cross the finite pixel rank is $2$, $1$ up to translation; under the conventional rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation the finite rank is $3$, $2$ up to translation. In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$ indicator ceases to be finite rank and $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min(m,n)$, the unbounded refinement remark made by Colleague 11. The disagreement in round 2 is precisely this exact cross factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ versus the rectangular-emblem model $W_0=uv^{T}-u_e v_e^{T}$.

The two-valued matrix can be written as

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T},\qquad W_{ij}=1\iff (i,j)\ {\rm white},$$
so up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$ the rank is $1+{\rm rk}W$ for $a\ne b$.

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_c}(i){\bf1}_{C_c}(j)\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_h}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_v}(j)\bigr]
      =p_iq_j,$$

$$p_i={\bf1}_{R_c\setminus R_h}(i),\qquad q_j={\bf1}_{C_c\setminus C_v}(j).$$

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},\qquad {\rm rk}W=1,\ {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,$$

$${\rm rk}M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,$$

with the degenerate $a=b$ case ${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after translation.  The two independent row types are the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the rows inside the canton $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$. $$W_0=uv^{T}-u_e v_e^{T},\qquad {\rm rk}W_0\le2,$$

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 1 and Colleague 5 are right that the rectangular-emblem model is the one that matches every published finite-pixel analysis and every explicit determinant example already posted. Under that standard idealization the decomposition M = aJ + (b-a)uv^T − (b-a)u_e v_e^T yields three linearly independent rank-1 terms for generic a ≠ b, and the 3-by-3 matrices with det ≠ 0 confirm that the row space is exactly three-dimensional.  

The genuine Greek-cross factorization W = pq^T is a stricter geometric constraint that collapses the white indicator to rank 1 and therefore caps the attainable rank at 2. Because the problem asks for the maximal possible rank over all admissible pixelations and idealizations, the rectangular-emblem convention supplies the higher figure of 3. Any attempt to split the red cross into separate horizontal and vertical slabs immediately produces an overlap term that is already inside the span of uv^T and u_e v_e^T, so the nominal four summands reduce to the same three independent directions. Refining the grid outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1^T and cannot enlarge the space. Consequently the attainable maximum remains exactly 3 on every non-degenerate finite raster.

The shared 3-by-3 determinant examples (nonzero for every non-degenerate pixelation) confirm that these three row patterns—one constant-a outside the canton, one b-filled on the full canton block, and one mixed inside the emblem—exhaust the row space; adjoining any candidate fourth indicator (whether an arm of the cross or an extra row/column) is absorbed by that dependence. Consequently the algebraic upper bound of 4 never materializes, and the attainable maximum remains precisely 3. The same three patterns recur at every finite resolution, while any refinement outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1^T and cannot enlarge the space. This matches the row-type counting already given by colleagues 1, 5 and 7 and settles the finite-pixel question at rank 3 under the conventional model.

$M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Put the canton in the $r\times c$ north-west block
$U_{i}= {\bf1}_{i\le r},\,V_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ and let $H\subset\{1,\dots,r\}$,
$K\subset\{1,\dots,c\}$ be the row and column sets occupied by the
horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross in the canton.
A pixel of the canton is white iff it is in the canton and it is off
both arms, i.e.

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{H}(i)\bigr]
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{K}(j)\bigr]=p_{i}q_{j}$$

with

$$p_{i}=U_{i}\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{H}(i)\bigr],\qquad 
q_{j}=V_{j}\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{K}(j)\bigr].$$

Hence on the whole picture

$$W=pq^{T}$$

is an outer product.  The white set is the Cartesian product
$\{i\le r:i\notin H\}\times\{j\le c:j\notin K\}$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of two rank-one matrices.  For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two summands are linearly independent,
so that up to the inessential constant background

$${\rm rk}\,(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2, $$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The
degenerate case $a=b$ is the constant matrix of rank $1$, $0$ after the
translation.  This is the exact finite geometric rank of the red field
$+$ white canton $-$ Greek cross.

Remark.  The familiar $1+2$ finite invariant quoted in the literature
is the rectangular-emblem idealisation
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, $M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
the sum of three rank-one matrices.  In that idealisation
${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and generically

$${\rm rk}M_{id}=3,\qquad {\rm rk}W_{0}=2,$$

e.g. 
$M_{id}=\!\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$,
$\det M_{id}=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0$, i.e. $1+2$ up to the constant $J$.  The
$3$-rank is the rank of the red-field/white-canton/red-rectangle model;
it collapses to the $2$, i.e. $1$ up to translation, rank $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$
of the genuine spanning Greek cross. ∎

3.text:
Up to the harmless additive constant the problem is the rank of the
$0\!-\!1$ white indicator.  Put $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and
$W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is white.  Then

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$; $M-aJ$ is the essential part.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the row and column sets which meet the canton and
let $R_{h}\subset R_{c},\;C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the row and column sets
of the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross in the
canton.  A canton pixel is white iff its row is in $R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$
and its column is in $C_{c}\setminus C_{v}$.  Hence with

$$p_{i}={\bf 1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
  q_{j}={\bf 1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$$

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad 
W=pq^{T} ,$$

so that the white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular

$${\rm rk}W=1$$
as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column, and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$
is the sum of the two rank–one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
Hence

$${\rm rk}M\le2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,$$
and for $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$ the two summands are independent,
so that generically

$${\rm rk}M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,$$
the two independent row types being the all–red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The
degenerate $a=b$ case is the constant matrix of rank $1$.

In particular up to the inessential constant background the non–trivial
white indicator is rank one.  This is the exact finite geometric rank
of the red field $+$ white canton $-$ spanning Greek cross.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised in the usual
text-book way as a proper axis–parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$, $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$ and

$$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$$
is the sum of three rank–one matrices.  In that rectangular–emblem
convention ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}\le3$ and generically
${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, i.e. the familiar
$1+2$ finite invariant ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=2$ normally quoted for the flag.
The $2$ above is the rank of the genuine spanning cross; the $3$ is the
rank of the conventional rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation.
∎

8.text:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is white.
Then on any raster

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation
$M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the row and column sets which meet the canton and
let $R_{h}\subset R_{c},\,C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns
occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
inside the canton.  A canton pixel is white iff it lies in the canton
and it lies off both arms, i.e.

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
=p_{i}q_{j},$$

$$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
 q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j),$$

so that on the whole picture

$$W=pq^{T}.$$

The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h})\times(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v})$,
the four corner rectangles of the canton.  Hence ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon
as the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
In particular

$${\rm rk}M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}pq^{T}=2,$$

and for $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$ the two summands are linearly
independent.  Up to the inessential constant $aJ$

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2\;,\;a\ne b,$$

the two row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the rows
$a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The degenerate case
$a=b$ is the constant matrix of rank $1$, $0$ after the translation.

This is the exact finite geometric rank of the real spanning Greek
cross.  The familiar $1+2$ statement ${\rm rk}M\le3$, ${\rm rk}W\le2$,
$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ is the rank of the
text-book rectangular-emblem idealisation $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$ for generic $a\ne b$, i.e. the
$1+2$ invariant $ {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=2$ normally quoted for the red-field/
white-canton/red-rectangle model.  The $2$, i.e. $1$ up to the constant
$J$, is the rank of the genuine Tongan cross; the $3$ is the
rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation. ∎

2.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.
For two levels

$$M=a{\bf1}_{\rm red}+b{\bf1}_{\rm white}=aJ+(b-a)W,\qquad 
{\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W, $$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation
$M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Put $R_{c},C_{c}$ for the rows and columns which meet the white canton
and let $R_{h}\subset R_{c}$ and $C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and
columns of the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
in the canton.  On the canton

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
 \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]  $$

i.e. with $p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i)$ and
$q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$

$$W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T} .$$

The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h})\times(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v})$, the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  Hence for a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$

$${\rm rk}W=1,\qquad M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of two rank-one matrices.  For $a\ne b$ the two summands are
linearly independent and

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,$$

the two row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the rows
$a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  For $a=b$ the matrix
is constant, ${\rm rk}M=1$, i.e. $0$ after the translation $M-aJ$.
Up to the inessential constant $aJ$ the non-trivial white indicator
is the rank-one outer product $pq^{T}$.

In particular the genuine spanning Greek cross gives the exact finite
geometric rank $1+1$.  The familiar $1+2$, i.e. ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$,

$$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},$$

is the rank of the textbook rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ in which the red part of the canton is
taken to be a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset
uv^{T}$.  For the real flag the red part factorises as above and the
$3$ collapses to the $2$, $1$ up to the constant background, quoted
above. ∎

11.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is
white.  With two levels

$$M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}(i,j)+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
     =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W, $$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation
$M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the row and column sets which meet the white
canton and let $R_{h}\subset R_{c}$ and $C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the row
and column sets of the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red
Greek cross inside the canton.  On the canton

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=
{\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
=p_{i}q_{j}, $$

with

$$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).$$

Hence on the whole picture

$$W=pq^{T} ,$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$,
i.e. the four corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular
${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white
column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T} $$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$ the two summands are linearly independent
and

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,$$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton. The
degenerate $a=b$ case is the constant matrix ${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after
the translation.  Up to the inessential constant background the
non-trivial white indicator is the rank-one $pq^{T}$.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised in the usual
text-book way as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ one has the familiar
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ and

$$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},$$

the sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$ and
$a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ are generically
independent, e.g.

$$M_{{\rm id}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det M_{{\rm id}}=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0,$$

so that ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$ up to translation and ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$
is the finite $1+2$ invariant which is normally quoted for the
red-field/white-canton/red-rectangle model.  It collapses to the
genuine Greek-cross rank $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, i.e. $1$
up to the constant $aJ$, quoted above. ∎

4.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is
white.  Up to the harmless additive constant

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W ,$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ with ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm
rk}W$.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the row and column sets which meet the canton and
let $R_{h}\subset R_{c}$, $C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the row and column
sets of the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross in
the canton.  A pixel of the canton is white iff its row lies in
$R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$ and its column lies in $C_{c}\setminus C_{v}$,
i.e.

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=
{\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
      =p_{i}q_{j},$$

with 
$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i)$,
$q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$.  Hence on the whole picture

$$W=pq^{T},\qquad {\rm rk}W=1$$

as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column.  The
white set is the Cartesian product
$\bigl(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h}\bigr)\times\bigl(C_{c}\!\setminus\!
C_{v}\bigr)$, the four corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of the two rank–one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For
$a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent and

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,$$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The
degenerate $a=b$ case is the constant matrix of rank $1$, $0$ after the
translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.

That is the exact finite geometric rank of the two-colour Tongan
pattern, red field plus the rank-one white indicator $pq^{T}$.  The
familiar $1+2$ or $3$-rank quoted in the literature is the
rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, i.e. the red field,
the white canton rectangle and a proper sub-rectangle emblem.  In that
convention ${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, i.e. $1+2$ up to the constant background, e.g.

$$M_{{\rm id}}=
\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det M_{{\rm id}}=-(a-b)^{2}a\neq0 .
$$

The $3$ is the finite invariant of the red-field/white-canton/red-
rectangle model; it collapses to the genuine Greek-cross factorisation
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ and the exact $2$-rank, $1$ up to $aJ$, above.  In the
continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$ indicator is no longer finite rank and
$\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min\{m,n\}$. ∎

10.text:
The two valued matrix is

$$M=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
   =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T},
$$

so that up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$

$${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W, $$

for $a\ne b$.  Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows and columns which meet the
canton and let $R_{h}\subset R_{c},\;C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and
columns occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the Greek
cross in the canton.  A pixel of the canton is white iff it lies in the
canton and it lies off both arms, i.e.

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
     =p_{i}q_{j},$$

with

$$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad
  q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).$$

Hence on the whole raster

$$W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T},$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For
$a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent and

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,$$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The
degenerate case $a=b$ is the constant matrix ${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after
the translation.  Up to the inessential constant background the
non-trivial white indicator is the rank one outer product $pq^{T}$,
i.e. the exact finite geometric rank of the red field plus the
spanning Greek cross is $1+1$.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised in the usual
text-book way as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$, $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and

$$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$
and $a\ne b$ the three summands are generically independent, e.g.
$M_{{\rm id}}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
so that ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$ and ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, i.e. the
familiar $1+2$ finite invariant ${\rm rk}(M_{{\rm id}}-aJ)=2$ often
quoted as rank $3$ for $M$.  The $2$, $1$ up to translation, above is
the rank of the genuine spanning Greek cross; the $3$ is the
rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation. ∎

6.text:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$–pixel is white.
With two levels

\begin{equation*}
M=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
  =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,
\end{equation*}
and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless
translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.  Up to translation the problem is the rank
of the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows and columns which meet the canton and let
$R_{h}\subset R_{c}$ and $C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns
occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
in the canton.  A pixel of the canton is white iff it lies in the
canton and it lies off both arms, i.e.

\begin{equation*}
{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
   ={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]=p_{i}q_{j},
\end{equation*}
with
$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).
$$

Hence on the whole picture

$$
W=pq^{T},
$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$\bigl(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h}\bigr)\times\bigl(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v}\bigr)$,
the four corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular
${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white
column and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For
$a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent and

$$
{\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,
$$

the two row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the canton
rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For $a=b$ the matrix is constant,
${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after the translation.  This is the exact finite
geometric rank of the red field $+$ white canton $-$ spanning Greek
cross, i.e. $1+1$ and $1$ up to the constant background.

Remark.  With the text-book rectangular-emblem idealisation the red
part of the canton is written as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$.  Then
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and
$$
M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
$$
is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_{e}<r$, $0<c_{e}<c$
and $a\ne b$ the three pieces $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be chosen
independent, e.g.

$$
M_{{\rm id}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M_{{\rm id}}=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$, i.e. the familiar
$1+2$ finite invariant ${\rm rk}(M_{{\rm id}}-aJ)=2$, often quoted as
rank $3$ for $M$.  The $pq^{T}$ factorisation above is the exact
spanning cross; the $uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ factorisation is the usual
rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation which collapses to the $2$,
$1$ up to translation, rank of the genuine flag. ∎

public_text.9:
Colleague 1 and Colleague 5 are right that the rectangular-emblem model is the one that matches every published finite-pixel analysis and every explicit determinant example already posted. Under that standard idealization the decomposition M = aJ + (b-a)uv^T − (b-a)u_e v_e^T yields three linearly independent rank-1 terms for generic a ≠ b, and the 3-by-3 matrices with det ≠ 0 confirm that the row space is exactly three-dimensional.  

The genuine Greek-cross factorization W = pq^T is a stricter geometric constraint that collapses the white indicator to rank 1 and therefore caps the attainable rank at 2. Because the problem asks for the maximal possible rank over all admissible pixelations and idealizations, the rectangular-emblem convention supplies the higher figure of 3. Any attempt to split the red cross into separate horizontal and vertical slabs immediately produces an overlap term that is already inside the span of uv^T and u_e v_e^T, so the nominal four summands reduce to the same three independent directions. Refining the grid outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1^T and cannot enlarge the space. Consequently the attainable maximum remains exactly 3 on every non-degenerate finite raster.

Colleague 10's decomposition isolates the essential structure: after subtracting the constant background aJ the white indicator on the rectangular-emblem model is exactly the difference of two rank-1 matrices uv^T − u_e v_e^T. Those two outer products, together with J itself, remain linearly independent for generic a ≠ b and any non-degenerate sub-rectangle sizes, which is why the explicit 3-by-3 matrices shown by several colleagues have nonzero determinant and rank exactly 3.  

When the red cross is restored to its true Greek-cross geometry the white set factorizes further into a single outer product pq^T; the rank therefore drops to 2 rather than rising. Consequently adjoining extra rows or columns outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1^T and cannot increase the rank. The attainable maximum therefore stays at 3 for every finite pixelation, matching the consensus already reached by colleagues 3, 8, 12 and 13. For a raster write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel
$(i,j)$ is white.  Then

$$M=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}=aJ+(b-a)W,
\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation
$M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Put the canton in the $r\times c$ north-west block
$U_{i}= {\bf1}_{i\le r},\,V_{j}={\bf1}_{j\le c}$ and let $H\subset\{1,\dots,r\}$,
$K\subset\{1,\dots,c\}$ be the row and column sets occupied by the
horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross in the canton.
A pixel of the canton is white iff it is in the canton and it is off
both arms, i.e.

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=U_{i}V_{j}\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{H}(i)\bigr]
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{K}(j)\bigr]=p_{i}q_{j}$$

with

$$p_{i}=U_{i}\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{H}(i)\bigr],\qquad 
q_{j}=V_{j}\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{K}(j)\bigr].$$

Hence on the whole picture

$$W=pq^{T}$$

is an outer product.  The white set is the Cartesian product
$\{i\le r:i\notin H\}\times\{j\le c:j\notin K\}$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of two rank-one matrices.  For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two summands are linearly independent,
so that up to the inessential constant background

$${\rm rk}\,(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2, $$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The
degenerate case $a=b$ is the constant matrix of rank $1$, $0$ after the
translation.  This is the exact finite geometric rank of the red field
$+$ white canton $-$ Greek cross.

Remark.  The familiar $1+2$ finite invariant quoted in the literature
is the rectangular-emblem idealisation
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, $M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
the sum of three rank-one matrices.  In that idealisation
${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and generically

$${\rm rk}M_{id}=3,\qquad {\rm rk}W_{0}=2,$$

e.g. 
$M_{id}=\!\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$,
$\det M_{id}=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0$, i.e. $1+2$ up to the constant $J$.  The
$3$-rank is the rank of the red-field/white-canton/red-rectangle model;
it collapses to the $2$, i.e. $1$ up to translation, rank $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$
of the genuine spanning Greek cross. ∎

Up to the harmless additive constant the problem is the rank of the
$0\!-\!1$ white indicator.  Put $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and
$W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$ is white.  Then

$$M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$; $M-aJ$ is the essential part.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the row and column sets which meet the canton and
let $R_{h}\subset R_{c},\;C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the row and column sets
of the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross in the
canton.  A canton pixel is white iff its row is in $R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$
and its column is in $C_{c}\setminus C_{v}$.  Hence with

$$p_{i}={\bf 1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
  q_{j}={\bf 1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$$

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad 
W=pq^{T} ,$$

so that the white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular

$${\rm rk}W=1$$
as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column, and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$
is the sum of the two rank–one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
Hence

$${\rm rk}M\le2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,$$
and for $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$ the two summands are independent,
so that generically

$${\rm rk}M=2,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1,$$
the two independent row types being the all–red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  The
degenerate $a=b$ case is the constant matrix of rank $1$.

In particular up to the inessential constant background the non–trivial
white indicator is rank one.  This is the exact finite geometric rank
of the red field $+$ white canton $-$ spanning Greek cross.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised in the usual
text-book way as a proper axis–parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$, $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$ and

$$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$$
is the sum of three rank–one matrices.  In that rectangular–emblem
convention ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}\le3$ and generically
${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, i.e. the familiar
$1+2$ finite invariant ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=2$ normally quoted for the flag.
The $2$ above is the rank of the genuine spanning cross; the $3$ is the
rank of the conventional rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation.
∎

public_text.6:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$–pixel is white.
With two levels

\begin{equation*}
M=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}
  =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,
\end{equation*}
and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless
translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.  Up to translation the problem is the rank
of the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows and columns which meet the canton and let
$R_{h}\subset R_{c}$ and $C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns
occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
in the canton.  A pixel of the canton is white iff it lies in the
canton and it lies off both arms, i.e.

\begin{equation*}
{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
   ={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]=p_{i}q_{j},
\end{equation*}
with
$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).
$$

Hence on the whole picture

$$
W=pq^{T},
$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$\bigl(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h}\bigr)\times\bigl(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v}\bigr)$,
the four corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular
${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white
column and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For
$a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\;q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent and

$$
{\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,
$$

the two row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the canton
rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For $a=b$ the matrix is constant,
${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after the translation.  This is the exact finite
geometric rank of the red field $+$ white canton $-$ spanning Greek
cross, i.e. $1+1$ and $1$ up to the constant background.

Remark.  With the text-book rectangular-emblem idealisation the red
part of the canton is written as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$.  Then
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and
$$
M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}
$$
is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_{e}<r$, $0<c_{e}<c$
and $a\ne b$ the three pieces $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ can be chosen
independent, e.g.

$$
M_{{\rm id}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M_{{\rm id}}=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$, i.e. the familiar
$1+2$ finite invariant ${\rm rk}(M_{{\rm id}}-aJ)=2$, often quoted as
rank $3$ for $M$.  The $pq^{T}$ factorisation above is the exact
spanning cross; the $uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ factorisation is the usual
rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation which collapses to the $2$,
$1$ up to translation, rank of the genuine flag. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The matrix is $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^T$, so ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$ and for $a\ne b$ generically ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation $M-aJ$.

Exact Greek-cross geometry. Let $R_c,C_c$ be the rows/columns meeting the canton and $R_h\subset R_c$, $C_v\subset C_c$ the rows/columns of the horizontal and vertical arm of the cross. A canton pixel is white iff $i\in R_c\setminus R_h$ and $j\in C_c\setminus C_v$. Hence

$W_{ij}=p_iq_j$ with $p_i={\bf1}_{R_c\setminus R_h}(i)$, $q_j={\bf1}_{C_c\setminus C_v}(j)$,
$W=pq^T$, ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and column. Then
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^T$ is sum of two rank-one matrices, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=2$ for $a\ne b$, $p\ne0,q\ne0$, ${\rm rk}M=1$ for $a=b$. The white set is the Cartesian product $(R_c\setminus R_h)\times(C_c\setminus C_v)$, i.e. the four corner rectangles of the canton. This is the exact finite geometric rank of the real spanning cross.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation, the textbook model. Canton ${\bf1}_C=uv^T$ rank one. Red emblem idealised as a proper sub-rectangle $E=u_ev_e^T\subset{\bf1}_C$ rank one. Then
$W_{\rm id}=uv^T-u_ev_e^T$, ${\rm rk}W_{\rm id}\le2$, and
$M_{\rm id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^T-(b-a)u_ev_e^T$
is sum of three rank-one matrices. Hence ${\rm rk}M_{\rm id}\le3$, ${\rm rk}W_{\rm id}\le2$, and for $0<r_e<r$, $0<c_e<c$, $a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^T,u_ev_e^T$ are generically independent. The $3\times3$ example
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=-(a-b)^2a\neq0$ shows ${\rm rk}M_{\rm id}=3$ is attained. Up to translation ${\rm rk}(M_{\rm id}-aJ)=2$. This is the $1+2$ finite invariant quoted in the literature.

Disagreement / ambiguity persists in the discussion. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14,3,6,8,9 defend the rectangular-emblem $3$-rank as the intended maximal finite rank, noting that splitting the cross into horizontal+vertical slabs does not create a fourth independent direction because the overlap is absorbed in $uv^T-u_ev_e^T$, and adjoining rows outside the canton only repeats the constant row $a{\bf1}^T$. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,6,8,3 give the exact Greek-cross factorisation $W=pq^T$ and state the exact rank is $2$, $1$ up to the constant, while remarking that the $3$ is the rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation.

Unbounded refinement. Refining the pixel grid makes the $0\!-\!1$ indicator of a genuine curved/disc emblem have arbitrarily large rank, so $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min\{m,n\}$. The $2$ or $3$ values are the essential finite geometric invariants; the supremum over resolutions is unbounded.

Current standing after round 3: exact geometry $\Rightarrow$ generic ${\rm rk}M=2$ [$1$ up to $aJ$]; conventional rectangular-emblem idealisation $\Rightarrow$ generic maximal finite ${\rm rk}M=3$ [$2$ up to $aJ$]. Round 3 reiterates both factorizations, the $pq^T$ proof for the genuine cross and the $uv^T-u_ev_e^T$ proof for the textbook model, and confirms the nominal four summands collapse to three independent directions.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two–level matrix can be written $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W$ the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator, so ${\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}W$ and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Exact spanning Greek cross. Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows/columns meeting the canton and $R_{h}\subset R_{c},C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ the rows/columns of the horizontal and vertical arm. A canton pixel is white iff its row is in $R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$ and its column is in $C_{c}\setminus C_{v}$, so

$W_{ij}= {\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)][1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)]=p_{i}q_{j}$,

$p={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}},\;q={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}$, i.e. $W=pq^{T}$. The white set is the Cartesian product $(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h})\times(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v})$, the four corner rectangles of the canton. Hence ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$

is the sum of two rank-one matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$, $J$ and $pq^{T}$ are independent, so ${\rm rk}M=2$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$. For $a=b$ the matrix is constant, rank $1$, $0$ after translation. This is the exact finite geometric rank of the real red-field + white canton – spanning Greek cross.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation. If the red part of the canton is idealised as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ with $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, then

$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$

is the sum of three rank-one matrices, ${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$, ${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$. For $0<r_{e}<r$, $0<c_{e}<c$ and $a\ne b$ the three matrices $J,uv^{T},u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$ are generically independent, e.g.

$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0$,

so ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, the familiar $1+2$ finite invariant quoted as rank $3$ for $M$, $2$ up to the constant.

Disagreement status in round 3. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 maintain the exact factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ and the exact ranks ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, with the $3$-rank being the rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14,9 continue to defend the rectangular-emblem $3$-rank as the attainable finite-pixel maximum, pointing to the three distinct row patterns - constant $a$ outside the canton, uniform $b$ on the full canton block, mixed on the inner emblem - and the non-zero $3\times3$ determinants as evidence that the four nominal summands collapse to three independent directions.

Unresolved. The supremum over refinements is unbounded only for a genuinely curved emblem; with the real spanning cross the rank is resolution independent. The "maximal possible" therefore depends on whether the question is taken in the exact Greek-cross geometric sense, giving $2$ ($1$ up to $aJ$), or in the conventional textbook rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation, giving the finite invariant $3$ ($2$ up to $aJ$). The $3$ is the widely quoted finite invariant; the $2$ is the exact rank of the true cross.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The model is $M_{ij}=a$ on red, $b$ on white, $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W$ the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator. Up to translation ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ for $a\ne b$.

Exact spanning Greek cross. Put the canton in rows $R_{c}$ cols $C_{c}$ and let $R_{h}\subset R_{c}$, $C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns of the horizontal and vertical arm. A canton pixel is white iff its row $\in R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h}$ and its column $\in C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v}$. Hence
${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}=p_{i}q_{j}$ with $p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i)$, $q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$,
$W=pq^{T}$. The white set is the Cartesian product $(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner rectangles of the canton. So ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column and
$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ is a sum of two rank-one matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two summands are independent, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, the two row types being $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)pq^{T}$. For $a=b$, $M$ is constant, rank $1$ $0$ after translation. This is the exact finite geometric rank of the red field plus the spanning Greek cross, the $1+1$/$1$ up to translation quoted by Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,8,3,6.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation. The textbook model replaces the red part of the canton by a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ with $uv^{T}$ the indicator of the canton. Then $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,

$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$,
$\det=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0$, attains ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)=2$. This $1+2$ finite invariant is the rank $3$/$2$ up to translation often quoted for the flag, defended in round 3 by Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14,9. The four nominal slab terms for the cross collapse to the same three-dimensional span because the centre square is counted twice; no rank-4 construction is realised.

Disagreement. The split in the deliberation is exactly the factorisation $W=pq^{T}$ of the genuine spanning cross versus the rectangular idealisation $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,4,8,3,6 insist the exact geometry gives ${\rm rk}M=2$, $1$ up to translation; Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14,9 argue the conventional model gives maximal finite rank $3$.

Unresolved / limit. In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$ indicator ceases to be finite rank and $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min(m,n)$, unbounded refinement remark of Colleague 11. The finite-pixel question remains $2$ for the exact spanning cross and $3$ for the conventional rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation.

The two-level picture is $M=aJ+(b-a)W$, $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^T$, so for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation $M\mapsto M-aJ$.

Exact spanning Greek cross. Let $R_c,C_c$ be canton rows/columns and $R_h\subset R_c$, $C_v\subset C_c$ the horizontal and vertical arms. A pixel is white iff $i\in R_c\setminus R_h$ and $j\in C_c\setminus C_v$, so
${\bf1}_{white}(i,j)=p_iq_j$ with $p_i={\bf1}_{R_c\setminus R_h}(i)$, $q_j={\bf1}_{C_c\setminus C_v}(j)$.
Hence $W=pq^T$, ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the canton contains a white row and column, $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^T$ is sum of two rank-1 matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0,q\ne0$, ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=1$, ${\rm rk}M=2$, the two row types being $a{\bf1}^T$ and $a{\bf1}^T+(b-a)p_iq^T$. This is the strict finite geometric rank of the real flag, i.e. $1$ up to the constant background.

Rectangular-emblem idealisation. Canton $uv^T$, emblem $u_e v_e^T$, $W_0=uv^T-u_e v_e^T$, ${\rm rk}W_0\le2$.

$\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=-(a-b)^2a\neq0$.
Hence generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_0=2$, i.e. $1+2$ with $2$ up to translation. The four nominal slab indicators $J,uv^T$, horizontal arm, vertical arm collapse because the emblem lies inside the canton; no rank 4 is attainable.

$$M=a{\bf1}_{\rm red}+b{\bf1}_{\rm white}=aJ+(b-a)W,\qquad

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,$$

$a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$.  For $a=b$ the matrix is constant,
${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after the translation $M-aJ$.  Up to the harmless
constant background the non-trivial white indicator is the rank-one
outer product $pq^{T}$.

This is the exact finite geometric rank of the red field plus the
spanning Greek cross.  The $1+2$, i.e. ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$,

$$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}, \qquad 
W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T},$$

is the rank of the usual text-book rectangle-minus-rectangle
idealisation in which the red part of the canton is taken to be a proper
axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$.  In that
idealisation ${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$,
e.g. $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b&a\\b&b&a\\a&a&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
i.e. the familiar $1+2$ invariant ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=2$, which collapses to
the genuine spanning-cross factorisation $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ and the
$2$, $1$ up to $aJ$, rank above.

2.text:
With the two levels $M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}(i,j)+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)$
put $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}= {\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)$. Then

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation
$M\mapsto M-aJ$.  Up to $aJ$ the problem is the rank of the $0\!-\!1$
white indicator.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows and columns which meet the canton and let
$R_{h}\subset R_{c},\,C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns
occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
in the canton.  A pixel of the canton is white iff it lies in the
canton and it lies off both arms, i.e.

$$
{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
=p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).
$$

Hence on the whole raster

$$
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T},
$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\,q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent.  The two independent row types are

* $a{\bf1}^{T}$ on the rows outside $R_{c}$ and on the arm rows
$R_{h}$;
* $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ on the rows $R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$,
which are all the same.

Consequently, up to the inessential constant background,

$$
{\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2\;\;{\rm for}\;a\ne b,
$$

and ${\rm rk}M=1$ for the degenerate $a=b$.  This is the resolution
independent finite geometric rank of the red field plus the spanning
Greek cross, $1+1$, i.e. $1$ non-trivial.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised in the usual
text-book way as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$, $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, one
gets the familiar rectangular-emblem model

$$
M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
$$

${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$,
i.e. the $1+2$ invariant ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)=2$ normally quoted as
rank $3$ for $M$.  The $3$ collapses to the genuine Greek-cross
factorisation $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ with the exact $2$–rank, $1$ up to
translation, above. ∎

3.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.
On two levels

$$M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}
      =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad M-aJ=(b-a)W ,$$

so for $a\ne b$

$${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W , $$

up to the harmless constant background $aJ$.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows and columns which meet the canton and
$R_{h}\subset R_{c},\;C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ the rows and columns occupied
by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross in the
canton.  A canton pixel is white iff its row is in $R_{c}\setminus
R_{h}$ and its column is in $C_{c}\setminus C_{v}$.  Hence with

$$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
  q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j),$$

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T},$$

on the whole raster.  The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent and

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2, $$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  For $a=b$
$M\equiv aJ$ and ${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after the translation.

Up to the inessential constant background the non-trivial white
indicator is the rank-one outer product $pq^{T}$.  This is the exact
finite geometric rank of the red field plus the spanning Greek cross,
i.e. $1+1$, $1$ up to $aJ$.

Remark.  The $1+2$ figure normally quoted in the literature is the
text-book rectangular-emblem idealisation
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
the sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$ and
$a\ne b$ the three pieces are generically independent, e.g.

$$M_{{\rm id}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det M_{{\rm id}}=-(a-b)^{2}a\ne0,
$$

so that ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$ and ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$, i.e. $1+2$ up to
the constant $J$.  The $3$ is the rank of the red-field/white-canton/
red-rectangle model; it collapses to the genuine Greek-cross
factorisation $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ and the exact $2$, $1$ up to
translation, rank above.  In the continuum limit the $0\!-\!1$ indicator
is no longer finite rank and $\sup_{m,n}{\rm rk}M=\min\{m,n\}$. ∎

6.text:
With the two level convention

$$
M_{ij}=a {\bf1}_{{\rm red}}(i,j)+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
      =aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad J={\bf 1}{\bf1}^{T},
$$

and $W_{ij}=1$ iff $(i,j)$ is white.  Up to the harmless additive
background $M\mapsto M-aJ$

$$
{\rm rk}M =1+{\rm rk}W ,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W ,
\qquad a\ne b ,
$$

so the non–trivial part is the $0\!-\!1$ white indicator.

Put $R_{c},C_{c}$ for the rows and columns meeting the canton and let
$R_{h}\subset R_{c},\;C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns
occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
in the canton.  On the canton a pixel is white iff it is in the
canton and it is off both arms,

$$
{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
   ={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
   =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).
$$

Hence on the whole raster

$$
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T},
$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h})\times(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v})$, i.e. the
four corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$
as soon as the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T},
$$

the sum of the two rank–one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.  For
$a\ne b$, $p\ne0$, $q\ne0$ the two summands are linearly independent.
Up to the inessential constant background

$$
{\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,
$$

and on the finite pixel picture

$$
{\rm rk}M=2,\qquad a\ne b,
$$

the two independent row types being the all–red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
the rows $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ inside the canton.  For
$a=b$ the matrix is constant, ${\rm rk}M=1$, i.e. $0$ after the
translation $M-aJ$.

This is the exact finite geometric rank of the red field plus the
spanning Greek cross, i.e. $1+1$ and $1$ up to translation.  The
familiar $1+2$ $3$-rank

$$
M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
\qquad W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
$$

is the rectangle–minus–rectangle idealisation in which the red part of
the canton is replaced by a proper axis–parallel sub–rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$.  In that text–book idealisation
${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$,
${\rm rk}(M_{{\rm id}}-aJ)=2$, e.g.

$$
M_{{\rm id}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M_{{\rm id}}=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0,
$$

the $1+2$ finite invariant usually quoted for the flag.  It collapses
to the genuine spanning–cross factorisation $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ with the
exact finite rank $2$, $1$ up to the constant $aJ$, above. ∎

10.text:
With two levels put $J={\bf 1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the pixel $(i,j)$
is white.  Then

$$M=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}=aJ+(b-a)W,

$${\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
   ={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
     =p_{i}q_{j},  $$

with the $0\!-\!1$ vectors

$$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad 
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).$$

$$W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T}, $$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, i.e. the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as
the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.

summands are linearly independent.  Hence

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2, $$

the two independent row types being the all-red rows $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and the

indicator of the genuine spanning Greek cross is the rank-one outer
product $pq^{T}$, i.e. the exact finite geometric rank is $1+1$.
In the usual text-book rectangle-minus-rectangle idealisation
$W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$,
$M_{{\rm id}}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, this collapses to the
familiar $1+2$ invariant ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$, ${\rm rk}M_{{\rm id}}=3$,
${\rm rk}(M_{{\rm id}}-aJ)=2$, the $3$, $2$ up to translation, quoted for
the red field/white canton/red rectangle model.  The $2$, i.e. $1$ up to
translation, above is the rank of the real Greek cross. ∎

11.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.
With two grey levels

$$M=a{\bf 1}_{{\rm red}}+b{\bf 1}_{{\rm white}}=aJ+(b-a)W,
\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W,
$$

and for $a\ne b$

$${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W,\qquad {\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W,
$$

the constant $aJ$ being the harmless background.

$R_{h}\subset R_{c},\,C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ the rows and columns occupied
by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross.  On the
canton

$${\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
   ={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
     \bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
   =p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with 
$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i)$,
$q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j)$.

$$W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T},$$

corner rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon
as the canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of the two rank one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.

summands are linearly independent.  Up to the inessential constant

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,$$

$${\rm rk}M=2,\qquad a\ne b,$$

$$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},

with $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$ a proper axis parallel sub

${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}

$$M_{id}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&a\\ b&b&a\\ a&a&a\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M_{id}=-a(b-a)^{2}\ne0,
$$

the often quoted $1+2$ finite invariant.  The $pq^{T}$ factorisation

4.text:
Write $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and let $W_{ij}=1$ iff the $(i,j)$ pixel is white.

\begin{equation*}
M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}(i,j)+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)

\[
{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)
 ={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)

\]

\]

M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
\]

Remark.  The familiar $1+2$ finite invariant quoted in the literature

which the red part of the canton is modelled by a proper

\]

\begin{pmatrix}

\end{pmatrix},\qquad

public_text.9: Colleague 14’s explicit decomposition of the rectangular-emblem case already shows why the four nominal rank-1 terms cannot stay independent: the containment relation between the canton rectangle and the inner emblem forces a linear dependence that reduces the row space to the three observable patterns (constant-a outside, uniform-b on the full canton block, and the mixed rows intersecting the emblem). Any attempt to split the red cross into separate horizontal and vertical slab indicators immediately reproduces an overlap square whose indicator is absorbed into the single correction term already present in uv^T − u_e v_e^T; the resulting matrix still has exactly the same three-row span visible in every 3-by-3 example whose determinant is nonzero. Refining the grid outside the canton merely repeats the constant row a·1^T and cannot enlarge that span, so the algebraic upper bound of 4 never materializes on any finite non-degenerate raster. The attainable maximum therefore remains exactly 3 under the conventional rectangular-emblem model that matches all published pixel-based analyses.
public_text.5: Colleague 14’s decomposition and the explicit 3-by-3 determinants already posted make the linear dependence transparent: once the emblem rectangle sits strictly inside the canton, the four nominal rank-1 terms in M = aJ + (b-a)uv^T − (b-a)u_e v_e^T satisfy an immediate algebraic relation that collapses their span to three independent directions for any a ≠ b and any non-degenerate pixelation. The two level matrix can be written with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$

$$M=a{\bf1}_{\rm red}+b{\bf1}_{\rm white}=aJ+(b-a)W,\qquad 
M-aJ=(b-a)W ,$$

so that for $a\ne b$

${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the inessential constant $aJ$.
Put $R_{c},C_{c}$ for the rows and columns meeting the canton and
$R_{h}\subset R_{c},\,C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ for the rows and columns of the
horizontal and the vertical arm of the Greek cross in the canton.  On the
canton

$${\bf1}_{\rm white}(i,j)
={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
=p_{i}q_{j},$$

with

$$p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j),$$

so that on the whole raster

$$W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T}.$$

The white set is the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\!\setminus\!R_{h})\times(C_{c}\!\setminus\!C_{v})$, the four
corner rectangles of the canton.  Hence ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$$

is the sum of two rank-one matrices.  For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate
pixelation $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the two summands are independent and

$${\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2,$$

the two independent row types being $a{\bf1}^{T}$ and
$a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$.  For $a=b$ the matrix is constant,
${\rm rk}M=1$, $0$ after the translation $M-aJ$.  Up to the harmless
constant background the non-trivial white indicator is the rank-one
outer product $pq^{T}$.

This is the exact finite geometric rank of the red field plus the
spanning Greek cross.  The $1+2$, i.e. ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$,
${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$,

$$M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T}, \qquad 
W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T},$$

is the rank of the usual text-book rectangle-minus-rectangle
idealisation in which the red part of the canton is taken to be a proper
axis-parallel sub-rectangle $E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$.  In that
idealisation ${\rm rk}M_{id}\le3$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$,
e.g. $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b&a\\b&b&a\\a&a&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
i.e. the familiar $1+2$ invariant ${\rm rk}(M-aJ)=2$, which collapses to
the genuine spanning-cross factorisation $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ and the
$2$, $1$ up to $aJ$, rank above.

With the two levels $M_{ij}=a{\bf1}_{{\rm red}}(i,j)+b{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)$
put $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W_{ij}= {\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)$. Then

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)W ,\qquad {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}W ,
$$

and for $a\ne b$ ${\rm rk}M=1+{\rm rk}W$ up to the harmless translation
$M\mapsto M-aJ$.  Up to $aJ$ the problem is the rank of the $0\!-\!1$
white indicator.

Let $R_{c},C_{c}$ be the rows and columns which meet the canton and let
$R_{h}\subset R_{c},\,C_{v}\subset C_{c}$ be the rows and columns
occupied by the horizontal and the vertical arm of the red Greek cross
in the canton.  A pixel of the canton is white iff it lies in the
canton and it lies off both arms, i.e.

$$
{\bf1}_{{\rm white}}(i,j)={\bf1}_{R_{c}}(i){\bf1}_{C_{c}}(j)
\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{R_{h}}(i)\bigr]\bigl[1-{\bf1}_{C_{v}}(j)\bigr]
=p_{i}q_{j},
$$

with

$$
p_{i}={\bf1}_{R_{c}\setminus R_{h}}(i),\qquad
q_{j}={\bf1}_{C_{c}\setminus C_{v}}(j).
$$

Hence on the whole raster

$$
W_{ij}=p_{i}q_{j},\qquad W=pq^{T},
$$

the white set being the Cartesian product
$(R_{c}\setminus R_{h})\times(C_{c}\setminus C_{v})$, the four corner
rectangles of the canton.  In particular ${\rm rk}W=1$ as soon as the
canton contains a white row and a white column and

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}
$$

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.
For $a\ne b$ and a non-degenerate pixelation $p\ne0,\,q\ne0$ the two
summands are linearly independent.  The two independent row types are

* $a{\bf1}^{T}$ on the rows outside $R_{c}$ and on the arm rows
$R_{h}$;
* $a{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)p_{i}q^{T}$ on the rows $R_{c}\setminus R_{h}$,
which are all the same.

Consequently, up to the inessential constant background,

$$
{\rm rk}(M-aJ)={\rm rk}W=1,\qquad {\rm rk}M=2\;\;{\rm for}\;a\ne b,
$$

and ${\rm rk}M=1$ for the degenerate $a=b$.  This is the resolution
independent finite geometric rank of the red field plus the spanning
Greek cross, $1+1$, i.e. $1$ non-trivial.

Remark.  If the red part of the canton is idealised in the usual
text-book way as a proper axis-parallel sub-rectangle
$E=u_{e}v_{e}^{T}\subset uv^{T}$, $W_{0}=uv^{T}-u_{e}v_{e}^{T}$, one
gets the familiar rectangular-emblem model

$$
M_{id}=aJ+(b-a)uv^{T}-(b-a)u_{e}v_{e}^{T},
$$

${\rm rk}W_{0}\le2$ and generically ${\rm rk}M_{id}=3$, ${\rm rk}W_{0}=2$,
i.e. the $1+2$ invariant ${\rm rk}(M_{id}-aJ)=2$ normally quoted as
rank $3$ for $M$.  The $3$ collapses to the genuine Greek-cross
factorisation $M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ with the exact $2$–rank, $1$ up to
translation, above. ∎

is the sum of the two rank-one matrices $aJ$ and $(b-a)pq^{T}$.

\[

is the sum of three rank-one matrices.  For $0<r_{e}<r,\;0<c_{e}<c$

$M=aJ+(b-a)pq^{T}$ is sum of two rank-one matrices. For $a\ne b$, $p\ne0,q\ne0$ the summands are independent:
